title: Inferring Experimental Objectives in Microscopy Experiments from Decision Traces
abstract: Modern microscopes can acquire, analyze and act on data far faster than human operators can decide what to measure next. Exploiting this speed in automated experiments requires the instrument to follow the scientific logic of the operator, and one way to encode that logic is through reward functions that become part of the operation process. Here we explore whether such reward functions can be learned from the decision histories of microscope operators. We propose multiple frameworks in which recorded choices among alternative measurement locations serve as comparative evidence about the operator's preferences, and we compare several algorithms for reconstructing the reward including interpretable linear models built on physically meaningful image descriptors, nonlinear functions of the same descriptors, an unsupervised image representation followed by preference modeling, and a preference trained deep kernel inspired model. The result of this analysis is a spatial field of reward functions over the sample that can be used to run the instrument. We also propose a way to benchmark these approaches, based on withheld decisions and on decision histories generated with known objectives. We then examine the possibility that a decision history contains changing priorities throughout the experiment. A hidden Markov model assigns distinct rewards to recurring selection strategies, whereas a continuous-state model tracks smoothly varying preference weights. Controlled sequences generated over real microscopy candidate sets show that both concealed switches and gradual drift can be recovered. These reward functions, learned directly from recorded decisions, provide candidate objectives for future automated microscopy experiments.

title: Estimating Silenced Tokens in Quantized LLMs
abstract: Quantization is the standard way to shrink large language models, and it is usually judged by perplexity and task accuracy. We ask a different question: after quantization, which words can the model still say at all? A token is silenced when no hidden state can make it the top choice of the output layer, so a greedy decoder can never produce it. We give a simple, scalable way to estimate how many tokens a quantized output head silences, combining three checks: a direction that lets a token win (so it is safe), an upper bound on how close a token's row is to being trapped inside the others, and an exact match that proves a token can never win. Each count is therefore a certified range: exact matches give its lower end and flagged tokens can only raise its upper end. In nearly all settings we report down to 3 bits the two ends coincide, so the counts are exact. Across three open models we find that quantization silences tokens: on large-vocabulary models it already appears at 8-bit precision, up to a few hundred previously reachable tokens on a 1B-parameter model, and grows as precision drops, while a small-vocabulary model resists until 3 bits. The loss is far from uniform across languages: on a multilingual vocabulary the silenced tokens are overwhelmingly non-Latin (Korean, Chinese, Thai, Arabic and Hebrew), even though Latin tokens dominate the vocabulary. Silencing is thus a measurable, language-sensitive side effect that standard averages miss, and it should be reported alongside them.

title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection
abstract: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.

title: Just Talk Once: Communication-Efficient Split Federated LLM Fine-Tuning on Edge Devices
abstract: Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning is increasingly shifting toward data generated on edge devices, where memory, computation, bandwidth, and connectivity constraints make conventional federated learning difficult to sustain. Split federated fine-tuning (SFT) improves client-side efficiency by offloading most model parameters and computation to the server but requires step-by-step bidirectional communication loop across the split interface and forces continuous client involvement throughout training. In this paper, we present L-shaped SFT, a split fine-tuning framework that removes this bidirectional bottleneck. Our key insight is that weight tying in modern LLMs enables server-side hidden activations to be directly supervised using target embeddings, allowing the training loss to be computed on the server without returning server outputs to the client. To further eliminate the need for continuous client participation, based on L-shaped SFT, we introduce one-shot SFT, in which clients upload activations once and then go offline while the server continues optimization over cached representations. We implement our design in a real system testbed with heterogeneous edge clients, including commercial smartphones and NVIDIA developer boards. Experiments demonstrate that our schemes significantly reduce communication costs and client online time compared with existing SFT baselines.

evidence.title: Just Talk Once: Communication-Efficient Split Federated LLM Fine-Tuning on Edge Devices
evidence.abstract: Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning is increasingly shifting toward data generated on edge devices, where memory, computation, bandwidth, and connectivity constraints make conventional federated learning difficult to sustain. Split federated fine-tuning (SFT) improves client-side efficiency by offloading most model parameters and computation to the server but requires step-by-step bidirectional communication loop across the split interface and forces continuous client involvement throughout training. In this paper, we present L-shaped SFT, a split fine-tuning framework that removes this bidirectional bottleneck. Our key insight is that weight tying in modern LLMs enables server-side hidden activations to be directly supervised using target embeddings, allowing the training loss to be computed on the server without returning server outputs to the client. To further eliminate the need for continuous client participation, based on L-shaped SFT, we introduce one-shot SFT, in which clients upload activations once and then go offline while the server continues optimization over cached representations. We implement our design in a real system testbed with heterogeneous edge clients, including commercial smartphones and NVIDIA developer boards. Experiments demonstrate that our schemes significantly reduce communication costs and client online time compared with existing SFT baselines.

title: Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head for Tiny Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Real-time onboard robot control calls for a lightweight vision-language-action (VLA) model, yet shrinking the backbone leaves less capacity for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter alternative by iterating in latent space before committing to an action, but existing designs refine a single undifferentiated state that must simultaneously encode slowly evolving task context and rapidly changing motor commands. We propose the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3-4.3x smaller than those of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC->D, at the lowest latency among compared methods. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and inference cost.

title: On the Interplay between Backtracking and Latent Confidence Directions in Reasoning Models
abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? Operating under the hypothesis that models maintain an internal representation of their uncertainty, we seek to extract this representation and characterize its relationship with backtracking behavior at answer proposals. By querying the model's verbalized confidence following answer proposals throughout a response trace, we extract a linear direction for latent confidence that separates high and low verbalized confidence. This direction can steer verbalized confidence as expected, but it surprisingly can also steer the next token probability of backtracking, performing on par with a linear direction extracted directly from backtracking examples. We then test the direction under progressively more realistic interventions. Steering continuously from a mid-trace answer proposal modulates response length (~-1.3k - ~+2.5k tokens) and the number of answer proposals (-4.18 - +4.75) in both directions, with minimal cost to accuracy. Applying the confidence direction from the start of generation, where proposal positions are unknown, still shortens traces at comparable accuracy, and its effect surfaces in the linguistic confidence of proposals. Overall, our study reveals the intricate interplay between a model's internal confidence and its proclivity to backtrack or commit to an answer.

title: Handling Data Heterogeneity in Edge IoT with Clustered Sequential Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning has emerged as an effective distributed solution to the limitations of centralized learning. It reduces the large volume of data that must be transferred to cloud servers when training machine learning models. Simultaneously, it improves privacy by allowing devices and users to keep their data locally. Instead of sharing raw data, only model updates, such as the gradients, are exchanged. However, it has limited performance at large scales, in contexts where data generated by thousands or millions of devices can be very heterogeneous and non-IID (non independent and identically distributed). In this paper, we propose a novel clustered sequential federated learning (CSFL) method, to address one of the main weaknesses of federated learning: data heterogeneity, which significantly impacts the convergence of the global model, as most existing methods fail to maintain good accuracy in highly heterogeneous environments. It's a hybrid approach that combines both sequential and parallel training in order to enhance accuracy, while accelerating the convergence speed of the global model. Based on clusters with balanced data distributions on each edge server, we train models sequentially using a knowledge distillation mechanism within each cluster to avoid catastrophic forgetting, aggregate them into an intermediate edge model, and finally combine all edge models in the cloud to produce a global model. We have evaluated CSFL through extensive experiments across various datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet) and various configurations, notably levels of heterogeneity. The proposed method consistently demonstrates strong convergence behavior in highly heterogeneous environments without introducing any additional overhead.

title: Notes on Generative AI for Mathematical Research
abstract: These notes describe how generative AI is now used to solve and to check research-level mathematics, with a focus on agents and their harnesses. For the proving agents Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos and the verification agent OSVerify, we explain the design principles, compare each with its base model, present case studies, and show how to use and contribute to them. We also briefly review the history of AI for mathematics and the community's reactions to it.

title: Layer-Level Control of Language Model Execution in Agent Frameworks
abstract: Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. We demonstrate the approach with a prototype that learns stitching bridges and state-conditioned execution policies from paired model states, then applies them during inference to select among continue, exit, and stitch. For dispatcher supervision, we select the least-computation action whose full-vocabulary next-token prediction matches the source model's full-depth prediction, using continue when neither early action matches. We train these components on a frozen proxy corpus of 5,000 typed-decision items authored using source texts sampled from WildChat conversations, then evaluate the prototype on JevBench measuring task accuracy, agreement with full-model predictions, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead. Preliminary results show an approximately 15% reduction in mean latency while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.

title: Neural Agent Compiler: Learning to Schedule Soft Dependencies
abstract: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $τ^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $τ^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

title: Practical Perspectives on Machine Learning Interpretability for Public Transport Demand Forecasting
abstract: As data generated in public transport systems are growing in complexity and quantity, machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to model and forecast transport demand. While often highly accurate, the adoption of these techniques for optimizing operations and supporting decision-making is impeded by their low interpretability, which leads to a lack of trust from transport authorities and stakeholders. The aim of this paper is to explore the real-world applicability of ML-based prediction methods by evaluating current approaches from the contradicting perspectives of accuracy and transparency. In particular, we perform a fair comparison of the inherently interpretable NeuralProphet time series model, with the post-hoc interpretation of XGBoost using SHAP on real-world data from the metro line M4 of Budapest. Our results demonstrate that XGBoost outperforms NeuralProphet in terms of forecasting accuracy. Additionally, we show that the insights from the post-hoc SHAP analysis align both with the seasonality components of NeuralProphet and the characteristic morphologies of transport demand time series, supporting the adequacy of using SHAP to provide transparency for accurate black-box models. Source code is available at: github.com/galigergergo/PTDemComp .

title: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Multi-Objective Bandits: Pareto Violations & Gap-Based Regret
abstract: We study Bayesian multi-objective bandits and ask an information-theoretic question: what aspects of an unknown environment must be resolved to achieve low regret? We show that the answer depends on the regret criterion and the information needed to represent its loss. For Pareto-violation regret, which incurs unit loss whenever a dominated action is selected, the Pareto-optimal set is a natural information target. We introduce a predictive separation measure for competing candidate Pareto sets, connect it to information gain about the unknown set, and use this connection to analyze Thompson Sampling and develop an Information-Directed Sampling strategy. We establish sublinear Bayesian regret under uniform and polynomially decaying separation and prove a lower bound showing that weak separation can impose an unavoidable statistical cost. We then study gap-based Pareto regret, which quantifies the magnitude of Pareto suboptimality. Here, Pareto-set information is generally too coarse: distinct environments can share the same Pareto set while inducing different reward geometries and Pareto gaps, and averaging environments consistent with one Pareto set need not preserve Pareto dominance. This motivates retaining finer information about the environment. We develop parameter-level information-theoretic analyses of Thompson Sampling and Information-Directed Sampling to derive gap-based regret guarantees. Under sublinear information budgets, Pareto Thompson Sampling also achieves sublinear gap regret while recovering the full Pareto set on the same run, with a related guarantee for a fixed mixture with gap-based IDS. Together, our results reveal a hierarchy of information requirements: binary Pareto membership can be controlled through set-level information, whereas quantitative Pareto-gap suboptimality can require finer knowledge of reward geometry.

title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal
abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.

title: Sharing of Irreversible Latent Features in lieu of RF IQ Data for Multiple Downstream Learning Tasks
abstract: Wireless in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) data is useful for training various radio frequency (RF) machine learning (ML) models. However, sharing such I/Q data faces barriers from concerns of (i) potentially violating laws related to recording raw samples that can eventually be decoded by an unauthorized third party, and (ii) revealing information about a proprietary system or the environment involved in the data capture. This paper proposes a different solution to sharing I/Q data intended for use in ML models by leveraging latent embeddings obtained through a shared encoder. The key contributions include: (i) demonstrating how a single set of common features can be extracted from an I/Q dataset for training multiple downstream RF classification or regression tasks, (ii) designing a method of structured noise infusion that impairs the reverse recovery of the raw I/Q from the feature space without significant impact to the downstream tasks, and (iii) demonstrating the application of this method on informative real-world, publicly available datasets. Sharing well-constructed yet privacy-preserving features can accelerate foundational research on ML for wireless without relying on hard-to-get I/Q samples.

title: Blind to What They Can Fix: A Detection Gap in Self-Improving Agents
abstract: AI agents can write programs that carry out a task without calling a model at every step, so the task runs fast and its logic stays open to inspection. Agents improve these programs by running them, studying their failures, and revising the code, a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We ask whether this process also yields runtime checks that can be trusted. In five task domains, with up to seven author models, agents bring their programs to high scores. Yet when the environment changes, the checks they were told to write stay silent on half or more of the resulting failures in four domains. These failures can be detected and repaired: a monitor built from records of normal runs catches most of them in three domains, and the same agents usually repair them once called. The checks do not examine the recorded relations that reveal the failures, and the strongest agent writes checks that catch most of them once told that its checks are the only thing that calls it back. An unreported failure stays unrepaired, which limits what self-improvement is worth in autonomous operation. Evaluations of self-improvement should measure not only scores but also whether a system notices its own failures.

title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement
abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.

In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.

title: CFANet: Learning Conflict-Free Weather Adapters for All-Weather Image Restoration
abstract: All-weather image restoration aims to recover clean images from diverse weather degradations such as rain, haze, and snow. Most existing all-in-one methods handle different weather types with a unified network or rely on single-label weather modeling. However, real-world adverse weather is often compositional, where multiple known weather primitives may coexist in a single image. To this end, we propose Conflict-Free Adapter Network (CFANet) for open-compositional all-weather image restoration. CFANet first employs a Weather Mixture Router (WMR) to predict non-exclusive composition weights for rain, haze, and snow from shallow features. Guided by these weights, a Shared-Private Weather Adapter (SPWA) dynamically composes a common adapter with weather-private adapters inside each Conflict-Free Adapter Block, preserving shared restoration capability while providing weather-specific residual adaptation. Moreover, a lightweight Natural Color Adapter (NCA) performs constrained color calibration to improve color fidelity and visual naturalness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive adverse weather image restoration performance and benefits downstream visual tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/wenchao-tech/CFANet-main

title: The China AI Registry
abstract: A registry by Satoshi Yamauchi (Japanese title: 988の名簿) that transcribes every row of the attachments (delta lists) to the notices "Generative AI services filed (and registered)" published by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC). Providing a generative AI service in China requires filing (备案) with the authorities, and the CAC publishes the filed and registered services with company names roughly every two months. Rows are transcribed from the attachment PDFs in their source column positions and characters; typos, column shifts and carry-overs are not corrected but recorded as observation codes, and each attachment is identified by the SHA-256 of its PDF. Only rows printed in an attachment PDF are admitted; no row is created from press reports, provincial cyberspace offices or company announcements, and every row of a connected attachment is admitted without exception. Each serial-number series is kept as its own table: filings, on-device filings, anthropomorphic-interaction filings, registrations and filing changes. Filing changes are appended without rewriting the original filing row. Only the author writes to the registry, with PGP-signed commits. The canonical data is data/registry.json; one CSV per table and data/sources.csv are generated from it. The data specification (docs/DATA_SPEC.md) and the update runbook (docs/UPDATE_RUNBOOK.md) are published with the data. The repository also contains a structural analysis of China's AI industry that uses the registry as its population, in Japanese and English editions. This archived version (v1.3.1, 22 November 2026) joins Attachments 1 to 14 (April 2024 to October 2026): as of 31 October 2026, 1,234 filings, 10 on-device filings and 1 anthropomorphic-interaction filing (1,245 in total, matching the CAC cumulative figure), 955 registrations and 1 filing change. Its text and data are identical to v1.3; v1.3.1 adds only the citation files. The CAC publication page is checked roughly once a month, and new attachments are joined when they appear. 中国の国家互联网信息办公室(CAC)が公告する「生成式人工智能服务已备案(和已登记)信息」の附件(差分名簿)の全行を転記した、山内怜史による台帳。中国では生成AIサービスの提供に当局への備案(登録)が要り、CACは備案・登記済みのサービスを社名入りで約2か月ごとに公告している。行は附件のPDFから原表の列位置と文字のまま転記し、誤字・列のずれ・混入は直さず観察コードとして記録する。附件はPDFのSHA-256で特定する。附件のPDFに書かれている行だけを収め、報道・地方の網信部門の発表・企業の発表からは行を起こさず、連結した附件の行は例外なくすべて収める。序号の系列ごとに1つの表とする(備案、端末側の備案、擬人化された対話の備案、登記、備案の変更)。備案の変更は、元の備案の行を書き換えずに追記する。台帳に書くのは著者一人で、コミットには署名を付ける。正本は data/registry.json で、表ごとのCSVと data/sources.csv はそこから生成する。データ定義(docs/DATA_SPEC.md)と更新手順書(docs/UPDATE_RUNBOOK.md)をデータとともに公開する。リポジトリには、この台帳を母集団にした中国のAI産業の構造分析(日本語版・英語版)も収める。この版(v1.3.1、2026年11月22日)は附件1〜14(2024年4月〜2026年10月)を連結しており、2026年10月31日時点で備案1,234行・端末側の備案10行・擬人化された対話の備案1行(計1,245行で、CACの公告の累計と一致)、登記955行、備案の変更1行を収める。本文とデータはv1.3と同じで、v1.3.1では引用情報のファイルだけを加えた。CACの公表ページは月に1回程度確認し、新しい附件があれば連結する。

title: Latent-Predisposition Personas for Heterogeneous and Reliable LLM Survey Simulation
abstract: LLM personas are used to simulate survey publics, which should reproduce not only answer distributions but also within-person coherence and stability. Drawing on mass belief systems research, we show that persona-conditioned LLMs produce over-constrained publics. Across three model families and three U.S. surveys, opinions on unrelated issues are 1.6-4.6 times as correlated as among humans, and party identification explains 2.5-7.6 times as much answer variance. Common remedies (temperature, diversity instructions, backstories) weaken these correlations by making answers more random. On Qwen, their ten-day test-retest reliability falls to 33-59% of the human level, and when made consistent they lose correlation fit. We propose Latent-Predisposition Personas (LPP), whose persons differ stably, not randomly. Each persona receives political engagement, value priorities, and party-relative issue deviations that grow as engagement falls. Answers are sharpened and calibrated to toplines and party crosstabs. At selected operating points, LPP is never significantly worse than any baseline and far more reliable. At matched human-level reliability, it has the lowest correlation error in all six model-survey combinations, also at a lower target. Errors still exceed those between human samples, and gains on framing effects and a frontier closed model are partial.

title: GeoFusion: An Uncertain Machine Learning Framework for Sensor Fusion
abstract: High positioning precision is a critical requirement in many Global Positioning System (GPS) applications, yet achieving it with affordable smartphone sensors remains an open challenge. Existing approaches treat each GPS observation as an absolute point, discarding the uncertainty inherent in the measurement conditions and leaving the cooperative potential of multiple phones observing the same location untapped. In this work, we propose GeoFusion, a three-stage uncertain machine learning framework for cooperative sensor fusion. In the first stage, each GPS observation is modeled as an uncertain object using one of two proposed models: the volcano function, grounded in satellite geometry, and the empirically derived mountain function, built from the statistical structure of real smartphone data. In the second stage, uncertain objects are clustered by location event using partitional and graph-based algorithms. In the third stage, the cluster output is refined using filter-based and learning-based estimators. Experiments on the Google Smartphone Decimeter Challenge dataset show that uncertainty modeling is a primary driver of precision gains: the mountain function significantly outperforms the geometry-only volcano function, and uncertainty-aware UK-medoids significantly outperforms its certain counterpart, k-medoids. A post-clustering deep neural network further refines the cluster estimates, and the recommended configuration achieves a mean absolute error of 2.90 +/- 0.15 meters on held-out test drives, comparable to and on average below the best reported single-phone precision of approximately 3 meters, demonstrating the potential of cooperative uncertainty-aware fusion for affordable GPS sensors.

title: Denoised but Not Improved: What EEG Denoising Does to a Downstream Task
abstract: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is routinely denoised before it reaches a downstream model, and the denoising literature scores a method by how closely its output matches a clean reference waveform. That reference does not exist for real scalp recordings: it is synthesized by adding artifact templates to signals merely presumed clean, and even an exact separation would return cortical activity blurred by volume conduction rather than the activity itself. Fidelity to it is therefore an unvalidatable objective, and whether it predicts any downstream benefit has gone largely unexamined. We report an audit that examines it. Holding a seizure-detection pipeline fixed and varying only the preprocessing stage, we find that five standard denoising methods, spanning analytic, cross-channel and supervised deep families, all fail to improve on the unprocessed signal, and most degrade it. To say what such a stage must instead do, we formalize a label-only, classifier-free probe that reads it by the separability geometry it induces on task-relevant features, decomposing any change into a between-class distance and a within-class scatter term. On a transform that does improve the task, the probe attributes the entire gain to a roughly one-quarter reduction of within-class scatter, with class separation statistically unchanged. What a downstream model benefits from is therefore variance suppression on task-relevant structure, which waveform-fidelity metrics neither measure nor reward.

title: Does Switching to Muon Hurt Fine-Tuning of Small Open Models? A Case Study on Qwen2.5-0.5B
abstract: Muon, an optimizer that orthogonalises the momentum update of each weight matrix, has become a strong alternative to AdamW for pretraining language models. Whether it should also be used to fine-tune the many open models pretrained with AdamW is less clear, and recent studies disagree: one reports a penalty for switching optimizers on a narrow task, another finds none in broad instruction tuning. Both rely mainly on models pretrained from scratch or on models of 4B parameters and above. I examine the question for a small, heavily trained open model, Qwen2.5-0.5B, fine-tuned with AdamW and with Muon on a narrow task (WikiText-2) and on broad instruction data (a Tulu-3 subset), with a separate learning-rate sweep for each optimizer and three seeds for every final configuration. Switching costs little on the target task: validation perplexity rises from 12.47 to 12.53 in the narrow setting, and the target loss does not get worse in the broad one. Forgetting, measured as the increase in loss on held-out web text, is almost entirely determined by how far fine-tuning moves the weights (r ≥ 0.998 across 38 runs), and at equal target loss Muon forgets 1.7–2.3 times more in the narrow setting. Muon saved 6% of peak GPU memory and ran 9–10% slower. At this scale I find little reason to switch.

title: A ROS2 based Human-In-The-Loop Framework for UAV Search and Rescue Operations
abstract: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.

title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
abstract: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

title: The Co-Development of Artificial Cognitive Capabilities: An Integrative Theoretical Framework of Interdependent Reconfiguration, Epistemic Warrant, and Future Reachability
abstract: The development of artificial intelligence is commonly characterized in terms of computational efficiency, model scaling, learning performance, generalization, and the successful execution of increasingly complex tasks. However, the emergence of autonomous agents, self-revising scientific systems, and open-ended learning architectures raises a more fundamental question: under what conditions does an intelligent system acquire genuinely new cognitive capabilities, rather than merely improve the efficiency of capabilities it already possesses?This article develops an integrative theoretical framework for understanding the co-development of artificial cognitive capabilities through functionally interdependent transformations. Its central proposition is that cognitive development depends not only on the performance of individual mechanisms of representation, action, observation, validation, and metacognitive regulation, but also on the organization of dependencies among these mechanisms.Drawing upon information theory, statistical comparison of experiments, active perception, causal representation learning, epistemic iteration, metareasoning, and open-ended learning, the framework distinguishes informational accessibility, operational capability, epistemically warranted capability, and the future reachability of cognitive capabilities.Several conditional results are developed through explicit formal constructions. First, complementary improvements may jointly enable a cognitive capability that remains inaccessible under either improvement separately. Second, locally advantageous decision rules may fail to discover productive developmental trajectories when benefits depend on coordinated transformations. Third, the order of cognitive transformations may affect developmental outcomes when operations involve prerequisites, noncommutativity, irreversible costs, or resource limitations. Fourth, agents possessing equivalent current capabilities may nevertheless differ in the range of capabilities reachable through subsequent development.The article further distinguishes functional improvement, epistemic progress, and developmental progress, demonstrating why improvements in internal evaluation scores cannot automatically be interpreted as genuine advances in cognitive capability.The proposed framework does not claim the discovery of a new law of information theory or a universal mechanism governing all forms of intelligence. Its contribution is integrative and explanatory: it provides a unified conceptual and formal structure for investigating how interdependent cognitive processes can jointly alter the accessibility, justification, and future development of artificial cognitive capabilities.

title: FedCRA: Client Risk-aware Aggregation via Update Reconstruction for IoT-based Federated Learning
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables distributed model training without sharing raw data, making it particularly suitable for Internet of Things (IoT) environments. However, FL remains vulnerable to poisoning attacks, where malicious clients manipulate local updates to corrupt global model optimization. Existing defenses mainly focus on updates within a single round and may confuse heterogeneous benign updates with malicious ones. In this paper, we propose FedCRA, a client risk-aware aggregation framework that exploits historical trajectories and trusted reference updates to reconstruct updates. Furthermore, the risk-aware aggregation jointly considers reconstruction gap, reference gap, and historical trajectory information to adaptively suppress suspicious updates. Extensive experiments under multiple poisoning attacks and heterogeneous data distributions demonstrate that FedCRA achieves stronger robustness than several representative aggregation methods while maintaining good scalability in large-scale FL.

title: Learning Gaussian Process Priors with Linear Semigroups and Kinetic Regularisation
abstract: We introduce a semigroup-based construction of Gaussian process (GP) priors. A linear semigroup transforms a source GP at $t=0$ into a prior at $t=1$, enabling computationally tractable regression. Linearity preserves Gaussianity, allowing us to characterise the evolution of the covariance and draw connections with optimal transport and convolution models. The semigroup is parametrised by its generator, which is learned through two competing objectives: the marginal likelihood encourages agreement with observations, while a kinetic-energy regulariser favours lower-energy trajectories and limits unnecessary mass displacement from the source GP. Experiments on independent GP draws show that, with sufficiently many training functions, the learned prior provides accurate predictions on held-out functions, while kinetic regularisation substantially reduces the energy of the generated trajectories without compromising prediction accuracy.

title: MM-DataLoop: Closing the Data-Side Loop for Recursive Self-Improvement in MLLM Post-Training
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a path toward improving models through repeated evaluation and revision. We study its data side in multimodal language model (MLLM) post-training, where heterogeneous operations and cross-round evidence must be coordinated. MMDataLoop organizes data interventions into five operation families and connects them through an Observe-Diagnose-Plan-Execute-Verify-Reflect cycle with shared rule memory. Across 34 candidate rounds on Qwen3.5-0.8B and five benchmarks, we hold the base initialization, shared training schedule and evaluation protocol fixed while varying data recipes. The five-benchmark mean reaches 63.04 at R33, up 5.32 points from the zero-shot baseline; R29, R32, and R33 form a close top cluster within 0.09 points. In eightcandidate comparisons, guided search reaches the preselected target in six candidates and identifies the top observed candidate, while random arms show higher means and lower dispersion. The selected R29 recipe also scores above two full-pool baselines under the same epoch schedule. Together, these findings establish MM-DataLoop as a traceable workflow and provide an empirical basis for studying how data-side decisions shape outcomes across MLLM post-training recipes.

title: LaSDAICVI: Children's Spanish Voice Commands Dataset
abstract: LaSDAICVI (LaSDAI Comandos de Voz Infantil) is a keyword-spotting dataset of Spanish speech recorded from 41 primary-school children aged 8 to 11 in Tucaní, Mérida state, Venezuela. It contains 29,061 isolated-word recordings (16 kHz, mono, 16-bit PCM WAV) of 60 keywords: the digits 0–9, the 32 results of the multiplication tables 2–9, and 18 voice commands. The release includes per-sample metadata (speaker ID, gender, age, grade), the official speaker-independent train/validation/test splits used in the thesis, background-noise clips for data augmentation, and the full B.Sc. thesis describing the recording protocol and baseline keyword-spotting models. Parents signed an informed consent form and each child signed an informed assent. The recordings are of minors: use them only for non-commercial research and education, do not attempt to identify participants, and do not use them for speaker identification, voice cloning or voice synthesis. Created at the Laboratorio de Sistemas Discretos, Automatización e Integración (LaSDAI), Universidad de los Andes, Mérida, Venezuela.

title: Strategic Client-Level Defense Placement in Mobile Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables mobile and edge devices to train jointly without centralizing private data, but compromised clients can poison the global model. When client-level protections cover only part of the population, a rational attacker can exploit predictable placement. We introduce SGDP-FL (Stackelberg Game-Based Defense Placement for Federated Learning), a budget-constrained Stackelberg game between a defender and an attacker. Before each round, the defender decides which clients to protect. The attacker observes this placement only through noisy reconnaissance, updates its belief about which clients are protected, and then chooses which clients to attack. We model the noisy observation as a Binary Symmetric Channel, and we model imperfect defenses by letting each protection block an attack only with a fixed probability. Monte Carlo estimation and a greedy knapsack oracle make the resulting bilevel problem tractable. We evaluate SGDP-FL on EMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 under IID and non-IID partitions. The evaluation covers single- and multi-client attacks, with attack targets either fixed or periodically reshuffled. In every tested setting, SGDP-FL achieves the highest mean accuracy among Random, Highest-Value, and UCB allocation. Under multi-client attacks with periodic reshuffling, it raises CIFAR-10 IID accuracy from 55.68% for the strongest baseline to 59.78%, and CIFAR-100 IID from 32.42% to 34.49%. It also transfers to label-flipping and backdoor attacks and complements robust aggregation.

title: Dimension Is Free, Horizon Is Not: When Evolution Strategies Rival Policy Gradients for LLM Fine-Tuning
abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO dominate LLM fine-tuning, yet recent work showed that Evolution Strategies (ES) also scale to fine-tuning models with billions of parameters. Which method needs fewer samples, and on which tasks, remains unclear. We view the two methods as estimators of the same gradient that differ in where they explore. Because ES perturbs parameters, its noise grows with the number of parameters, and because PG samples actions, its noise grows with the number of generated tokens. Only noise along the directions that change the reward slows learning. The cost of ES then depends on the effective dimension, the number of independent skills a task requires rather than its parameter count, while the cost of PG depends on the effective horizon, which counts only the tokens that share both credit and weights with the reward-carrying ones. We train both methods on a synthetic task where the number of skills and the effective horizon can be varied separately. PG is cheaper when the horizon is short, ES becomes cheaper once it is long enough, and this crossover moves to longer horizons as the number of skills grows. We then measure the effective horizons of 20 NLP, math reasoning, and agentic tasks and compare the two methods with Qwen2.5-7B. PG leads on short-horizon tasks, the two tie on the moderate-horizon math ones, and no task has a horizon in the regime where the theory predicts an ES advantage. Terminal-Bench has a far longer horizon. There, in a preliminary comparison with Qwen3.5-4B, ES without any credit assignment reaches a higher success rate than the PG checkpoint released with Tmax, as the theory predicts. ES should thus have the advantage on long-horizon tasks with few independent skills and a nonvanishing reward signal. Current benchmarks are only at the onset of this regime, so ES should become more competitive as agentic tasks grow longer.

title: CoHABIT: Complementary Evaluation of Furniture Layouts through Spatial Rules and Household Routines
abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.

title: From Black-Box Computation to Causal Accessibility: Toward a Theory of Emergent Cognitive Capabilities in Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The increasing capabilities of artificial intelligence systems have intensified a fundamental question concerning the nature of machine intelligence: how can computational systems acquire cognitive capabilities that were neither explicitly programmed nor fully anticipated by their designers? Conventional explanations emphasize architectural complexity, parameter scaling, optimization, distributed representations, and the acquisition of increasingly sophisticated computational algorithms. Although these perspectives have substantially advanced the understanding of artificial intelligence, they do not completely resolve the distinction between information encoded within a system and information that can be functionally employed in generating intelligent behavior. This paper develops a theoretical framework centered on causal accessibility, defined as the context-dependent capacity of internally represented information to participate causally in task-relevant computational operations. The central hypothesis is that some changes in cognitive capability may arise not from the acquisition of fundamentally new representations or operations, but from changes in the functional accessibility, coordination, and compositional reuse of existing computational resources. The framework distinguishes representational availability, decodability, causal accessibility, compositional usability, and behavioral realization. It introduces a formal account of capability elicitation under fixed model parameters and specifies the conditions under which internal causal interventions could distinguish genuine functional access from mere informational correlation. Three theoretical propositions clarify why encoded information need not be behaviorally usable, why changes in accessibility can alter task performance without parameter modification, and why behavioral equivalence does not imply mechanistic equivalence. The proposed framework is situated in relation to mechanistic interpretability, causal abstraction, in-context learning, global workspace models, and theories of compositional intelligence. Its potential contribution is an integrated explanatory account of how latent computational resources may become operative cognitive capabilities. The paper does not claim to establish a novel fundamental law or provide new empirical findings. Instead, it offers a theoretically explicit and potentially falsifiable research program for investigating capability formation, emergence, and the organization of artificial intelligence.

title: PRISM: Reinforced Semantic Communication for Decentralized Federated Anomaly Detection in Vehicular Networks
abstract: Decentralized Federated Learning (DFL) enables collaborative learning that preserves privacy, but faces critical communication challenges in bandwidth-constrained environments such as vehicular networks. We propose Policy-driven Representation and Information Selection Method (PRISM), a Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based method that optimizes semantic communication in DFL through adaptive representation selection and intelligent topology management. Our dual-model architecture separates task learning (autoencoder-based anomaly detection) from communication control (Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based decision making), enabling agents to dynamically select between transmitting full model weights or compressed trajectory embeddings. We formulate this as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and train using a Centralized Training Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm. We demonstrate our method through a digital twin monitoring scenario where vehicles collaboratively detect trajectory anomalies in neighbors' behavior in real time, and the logged detections support forensic analysis, insurance claims, and fleet auditing. Experiments on Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) generated Barcelona traffic data show an F1-score of 0.90, scaling from 2 to 128 agents with graceful degradation past N = 32, Byzantine-robust aggregation, and validation on Next Generation Simulation (NGSIM) US-101 real traces (F1 0.82). The learned policy exhibits emergent temporal behavior: transmitting weights early during training when model divergence is high, then shifting to embeddings as models converge, with the weight-to-embedding mix derived as the equilibrium of the communication budget constraint. The method generalizes to other bandwidth-limited collaborative learning domains.

title: Learning Global Probabilistic Explanations
abstract: Interpreting the predictions of complex black-box classifiers remains a central challenge in explainable artificial intelligence. While local explanations clarify individual predictions, there is a significant need for global probabilistic explanations that capture a model's overall behavior across the input distribution. Such an explanation is a small subset $K$ of features, whose relevance is measured by the expected probability, over a random input $\mathbf x$, that the classifier assigns the same label to $\mathbf x$ and to a random input agreeing with $\mathbf x$ on $K$. In this study, we investigate the task of identifying maximally relevant global explanations under a cardinality constraint, focusing on product distributions with full support on discrete feature spaces. We introduce a spectral explainer that leverages membership queries to the black-box classifier and employs Fourier-analytic, junta-learning methods to produce probably approximately correct (PAC) explanations. Our algorithm is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the explanation size limit, maximum feature cardinality, and desired accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the theoretical guarantees and show that the spectral explainer outperforms a greedy baseline as the explanation size increases.

title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
abstract: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.

title: When to Trust a Knowledge-Graph Walk: An Empirical Study of Per-Hop Decision Confidence
abstract: LLM-based question answering over knowledge graphs is accurate but expensive, and it rarely says when an answer is likely wrong. We study an old design, in which each hop of a walk is a classification over the current node's relations plus STOP, with a zero-shot, swappable decider, and ask what the walk's path confidence is worth on MetaQA, WebQSP, CWQ and a 2WikiMultiHopQA evidence graph. Where walks fail often enough to matter (MetaQA 3-hop, WebQSP), path confidence ranks right above wrong answers well (AUROC 0.82-0.97): the most confident half of MetaQA 3-hop answers is 99% accurate (81% overall). With the model and prompt fixed, reading token probabilities beats stated confidence by 0.09-0.23 AUROC and matches or beats 5-sample voting at a fifth of its cost. Raw confidence is overconfident, but a two-parameter Platt fit repairs much of that. The walk is less accurate than an LLM writing the relation path in one call, cheaper only on Freebase, and its confidence fails on CWQ. On 2Wiki, walks that never reached a decision were scored as certain; scoring them lowest lifts AUROC from 0.67 to 0.92, and to 0.85 on a held-out sample. As a strong agent's tool, the walk cuts cost by 17% at equal accuracy. The library, every run and the table scripts are released at https://github.com/manvirchakal/graphwalk.

evidence.title: When to Trust a Knowledge-Graph Walk: An Empirical Study of Per-Hop Decision Confidence
evidence.abstract: LLM-based question answering over knowledge graphs is accurate but expensive, and it rarely says when an answer is likely wrong. We study an old design, in which each hop of a walk is a classification over the current node's relations plus STOP, with a zero-shot, swappable decider, and ask what the walk's path confidence is worth on MetaQA, WebQSP, CWQ and a 2WikiMultiHopQA evidence graph. Where walks fail often enough to matter (MetaQA 3-hop, WebQSP), path confidence ranks right above wrong answers well (AUROC 0.82-0.97): the most confident half of MetaQA 3-hop answers is 99% accurate (81% overall). With the model and prompt fixed, reading token probabilities beats stated confidence by 0.09-0.23 AUROC and matches or beats 5-sample voting at a fifth of its cost. Raw confidence is overconfident, but a two-parameter Platt fit repairs much of that. The walk is less accurate than an LLM writing the relation path in one call, cheaper only on Freebase, and its confidence fails on CWQ. On 2Wiki, walks that never reached a decision were scored as certain; scoring them lowest lifts AUROC from 0.67 to 0.92, and to 0.85 on a held-out sample. As a strong agent's tool, the walk cuts cost by 17% at equal accuracy. The library, every run and the table scripts are released at https://github.com/manvirchakal/graphwalk.

title: S hear : Goal-Oriented Anomaly Detection on Compressed Time Series via Semantic Transition Graph
abstract: Sensor data in IoT systems are commonly compressed to meet resource constraints, yet anomaly detection directly on compressed data remains largely unexplored. This challenge is particularly evident for recurrent anomalies, which commonly appear as repeated abnormal patterns in long-running IoT streams. Existing approaches often become cumbersome or expensive since they decouple compression from analytics, requiring detection to reprocess full raw data, while supervised deep learning alternatives further demand labels or incur computational overhead unsuitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose Shear, a goal-oriented unsupervised method via Semantic Transition Graph (STG) induced directly from compressed time series. The STG organizes compressed representation as semantic states and encodes their temporal transitions, so that recurrent anomaly patterns are identified through unlikely state transition chains without decompression or neural network inference. Experiments on public datasets show that Shear achieves better detection performance than state-of-the-art approaches, while running 3.9× to 11.2× faster than subsequence-oriented methods and up to 2219× faster than deep learning baselines, with substantially reduced storage and memory footprint.

title: A Cascaded Framework with a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN Model for Pre- and Post-Treatment Glioma Segmentation
abstract: Accurate glioma segmentation is vital for diagnosis and follow-up, but manual segmentation is time-consuming, subjective, and variable across interpreters. Gliomas are heterogeneous in size, shape, and location. Deep learning has therefore emerged as a potential solution. CNNs excel at local features but may struggle with long-range dependencies, whereas Vision Transformers capture global context efficiently but incur higher computational complexity. Most previous studies focused on pre-treatment gliomas; post-treatment cases with resection cavities (RCs) remain less explored. This study proposes a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN (CMC-Seg) model within a cascaded framework for pre- and post-treatment diffuse glioma segmentation, aiming to balance accuracy and computational cost. Experiments used BraTS 2025 mpMRI of diffuse glioma patients. After preprocessing, a coarse segmentation model extracted tumor-centered patches, which were fed to CMC-Seg for fine-grained segmentation. CMC-Seg was compared with 3D U-Net, SegResNet, SwinUNETR, UNETR, nnFormer, and SegMamba. On the test set, CMC-Seg achieved the highest mean Dice (81.20%) and non-enhancing tumor core (NETC) Dice (77.09%). It also achieved an RC Dice of 78.63% and the lowest 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95; 4.39 mm). Results were comparable to CNN and Mamba baselines and significantly better than Transformer-based baselines (P < 0.05). CMC-Seg required the fewest inference GFLOPs (381.49). Ablation experiments indicated that multi-direction scanning and cross-attention improved performance, particularly for RC (P < 0.05). Grad-CAM explainability experiments showed that CMC-Seg focuses on diagnostically relevant tumor regions.

title: Meddies-PII: A Multilingual Framework for Personally Identifiable Information Extraction in Clinical De-identification
abstract: Multilingual PII extraction in clinical text is limited by scarce governed data and by synthetic corpora whose construction is thinly documented. We present a large multilingual dataset covering seventeen languages, including seven Southeast Asian languages, and nine PII labels. We also document a detailed generation pipeline and release the complete prompts, catalogues, checks and label maps. A compact 350M-parameter BIOES token classifier trained on the resource achieves the highest score on all fifteen public benchmarks, significantly ahead of the strongest of four public systems on fourteen of them, with a mean exact-match F1 of 0.827 against 0.672 for the strongest system. We also tested it, without adaptation, on multilingual benchmarks, including two human-annotated German and Spanish clinical-style corpora, where it is competitive with the best public systems once annotation conventions are aligned, and is best in four of ten MultiGraSCCo languages; the results show that performance transfers across public benchmarks. We also analyse the data and find almost no near-duplicates and no text overlap between training and any evaluation set. The dataset, benchmark, model, generation framework and evaluation code are planned for public release upon acceptance.

title: The norm axiom and factor hyperfields
abstract: Touchard and the author asked whether every valued hyperfield, in Krasner's sense with the norm axiom, is of the form H_ρ(K): a valued field K read up to relative error ρ. The question turns on the norm axiom. If a valued hyperfield is a quotient K^times/Tcup{0} of a field, the norm axiom forces T=1+m_ρ for a valuation on K. This completes the proof of a published proposition, and it makes the question equivalent to asking whether every Krasner valued hyperfield is such a quotient. For value group Z we prove directly that it is. Without the norm axiom the answer is negative. Layering a hyperfield over a non-trivial ordered abelian group gives a factor hyperfield exactly when the hyperfield itself is one, so Massouros's hyperfields yield hyperfields with a non-trivial valuation, satisfying all the other axioms, that are not factor hyperfields. The general question remains open.

title: Tissot indicatrix for location encoders: Characterizing local distortion in learned geographic embeddings
abstract: With the increasing adoption of geographic artificial intelligence, location encoders are widely used to map geographic coordinates to learned embeddings for tasks in Earth observation and geospatial modeling. Similar to map projections, location encoders can distort geographic space, that is, equal-distance displacements in different directions can result in unequal embedding changes. However, such distortion remains largely unexamined, and it can propagate into downstream applications. We adapt Tissot's indicatrix, a cartographic tool for map projection distortion, to characterize this distortion. At each location, we compare encoder outputs at equal distances in 32 directions and fit a tensor, represented by an ellipse, whose elongation (anisotropy) and orientation describe the local distortion. The fit requires only encoder outputs without access to model internals and is validated against references with known geometry. By applying the method to thirteen released checkpoints of five encoder families, we find that distortions vary across space and inherit the input geometry to varying degrees, closely in GeoCLIP with its Equal Earth input (anisotropy correlation of 0.88) and weakly or moderately in the other encoders. The distortion also affects the locations an encoder treats as neighbors. Within 1km of 20 query sites, the 40 nearest neighbors in geographic and embedding space overlap by a median of only 57.5--87.5% across the checkpoints, while the fitted ellipses select exactly the same embedding neighbors in 265 of 299 comparisons. These findings provide a geographic basis for assessing location encoders, and the accompanying eTissot package implements the methods for user-specified encoders.

title: Joint Optimizing Federated Learning and Unlearning over Wireless Networks
abstract: In this paper, a communication and energy-efficient federated learning (FL) and unlearning (FU) co-designed framework is proposed. In the considered model, multiple edge devices collaboratively train a model. Users are allowed to quit the FL training and remove their data impacts on the trained model. Hence, an FU training is performed after the FL training. To reduce the energy and time consumption of FU, the users are grouped into multiple clusters such that the users in a group will retrain a deep learning model when the users in the group request to quit the FL training. The base station (BS) needs to determine the number of clusters, the users in each cluster, and the resource block (RB) allocated to each user, according to the probability that each user requests to quit the FL, data distribution, wireless channel conditions, and time and energy constraints. This problem is formulated as an optimization problem whose goal is to minimize the expected loss by determining the number of clusters, user cluster assignment, and RB allocations. This problem is challenging to solve since 1) the BS cannot predict which users will request data deletion in advance and 2) no explicit equation exists to capture the relationship between the number of clusters, user cluster assignment, and the expected FU loss. To solve the formulated problem, we first analyze the convergence rate of FU to build an explicit relationship among the FU training loss, the number of clusters, and the users in each cluster. Based on this relationship, the original problem is simplified to a mixed-integer optimization problem which can be divided into the user cluster assignment and the RB allocation optimization subproblems. These two problems are alternately solved by the designed Dinkelbach's method and the fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (Dinkelbach-FISTA) and the standard Hungarian algorithm. Simulation results show that our method improves classification accuracy by up to 11.1% and achieves up to 3× faster convergence compared to gradient-based and ISTA-based methods.

title: Tabular Foundation Models for Weighted Regression and Classification
abstract: Weighted regression and classification have applications ranging from missing-data analysis and causal inference to insurance pricing and particle physics. Existing weighted methods must be fitted and tuned on each dataset, which is costly for flexible nonlinear learners. Tabular foundation models avoid this cost. A Transformer is pretrained once on many simulated datasets and then predicts on a new dataset by in-context learning, using its observations as context without further fitting. Recent models such as TabPFN-3.5 surpass tuned conventional methods, but they cannot use sample weights. We develop a general pipeline that adapts such models to weighted prediction through weighted attention, a normalized weighted loss, and pretraining on synthetic weighted prediction tasks from missing-data problems. Applied to TabPFN-3.5, it yields WeightedPFN, which performs strongly on real datasets, both in missing-data problems and in out-of-distribution causal tasks, while running about as fast as linear baselines. We also establish a statistical theory showing that a suitably pretrained weighted Transformer attains the nonparametric minimax rate for weighted regression on new datasets without further fitting.

title: CAR: Reducing Decoder Output Shift in Visual Token Pruning via Coverage Selection and Attention Reallocation
abstract: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods degrade substantially under aggressive pruning, especially on visual grounding (VG). We analyze the sources of this degradation from the perspective of the output shift that pruning causes in decoder layers, and decompose this shift in closed form into two terms, an image summary error and an attention allocation error. The summary error stems from the loss of visual information, and the allocation error from the drop in the share of attention assigned to visual tokens. To reduce both errors, we propose CAR (Coverage selection and Attention Reallocation), a token pruning framework that restores attention share while maintaining information. Specifically, to minimize the summary error, whose upper bound tightens as the retained tokens better cover all visual tokens, our coverage selection retains tokens that are both salient and non-redundant, with saliency from encoder heads chosen by a label-free probe. To minimize the allocation error, our attention reallocation reassigns the attention of the discarded tokens to the retained ones through a closed-form logit bias. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B with $90\%$ of the visual tokens pruned, CAR retains $93.0\%$ of the unpruned accuracy on visual question answering (VQA) and $77.9\%$ on VG, against $26.5\%$ for the best existing method on VG; the logit bias alone raises the VG accuracy of existing methods by up to $24$ points. Experiments on multiple MLLMs across VQA, VG and video understanding show that CAR generalizes well and consistently outperforms existing methods.

title: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents
abstract: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47--90.90\%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46\% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.

title: Replication code for: Censoring-aware positive-unlabeled learning and calibrated triage for longitudinal financial statement fraud detection
abstract: Clean Python reference implementation, verification tests, and publication plotting scripts accompanying Censoring-aware positive–unlabeled learning and calibrated triage for longitudinal financial statement fraud detection (CA-FRC: Censoring-Aware Financial Forensic Risk and Calibration). Contents: ca_frc.py: Complete CA-FRC Modules 1–3 implementation (RightTruncatedLagEstimator, capu_risk_and_derivatives, NativeNaNHistogramGBDT, BoundedPUPlattCalibrator, compute_epistemic_triage_score, CAFRCPipeline, and five-block accounting-identity attribution grouping). smoke_test.py: Five deterministic unit and end-to-end checks (<1 s) without external data dependencies. plot_figures.py: Generates manuscript multi-panel PDF Figures 2–5 from aggregated evaluation tables. requirements.txt and README.md: Python 3.10+ dependencies, module-to-equation mapping, and public benchmark input schemas (SEC AAER panel and UCI Polish bankruptcy). title: Poster: ProbeGuard, Budgeted Active Probing for Safe LLM Service Recomposition under Silent Semantic Drift
abstract: Under silent semantic drift, an upgraded edge-cloud service stays schema-compatible but changes a unit, precondition, or state transition, invalidating LLM-orchestrated compositions. ProbeGuard treats candidate behaviors as a version space and spends a small budget of safe probes to discriminate them; owner-protected executable clauses cannot be weakened by an LLM, and a service is cleared only when all evidence-compatible hypotheses agree. In 252 controlled episodes, hybrid hypothesis generation recovers 94.8% of drifted behaviors, and ProbeGuard automates 98.4% of decisions correctly while cutting harmful clearance from 5.3% to 2.7% and latency from 0.94 to 0.56 s versus the strongest deployable baseline.
