title: Beyond Language Optimization: Enhancing Visual Representations for Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Accurate chest X-ray radiology report generation (RRG) requires recognizing clinically relevant abnormalities and accurately describing them. Although Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves the clinical accuracy of generated reports, our analyses suggest limited improvements in visual representations for abnormality recognition. To address this limitation, we propose a selective regional visual distillation framework that enhances visual representations of challenging abnormalities while preserving existing visual capabilities. Specifically, we train a region-aware teacher with targeted supervision on challenging anatomical regions to acquire complementary visual knowledge. Rather than transferring all teacher features, we verify their utility through regional feature replacement and select only those that improve the original student's performance. We further introduce a Spatially Gated Residual Adapter (SGRA) to distill these verified features while minimizing interference with the student's existing visual representations. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray demonstrate improved clinical report accuracy and region-level abnormality recognition across different multimodal large language model backbones, while largely preserving performance on non-target findings.

title: Vanishing Initialization Turns Diagonal Tensor Gradient Flow into Greedy Matching
abstract: We study gradient-flow (GF) learning of tensors from vanishing initialization in canonical polyadic (CP) factorization models. For tensors of order $ν\geq3$ whose targets are diagonal in mode-wise orthonormal bases, we prove that the limiting learning dynamics follows a simple greedy bipartite matching process. Each rank-one component of the model, called an atom, can potentially learn each rank-one component of the target, called a scalar sector. title: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents
abstract: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.

title: PQ-FL-IDS: A Post Quantum Safe Federated Edge Intrusion Detection Scheme underlying 6G
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables Intrusion Detection System (IDS) models to be trained across Sixth Generation (6G) edge nodes without transferring sensitive traffic records to a central server. However, the model updates exchanged during FL-based IDS (FL-IDS) training remain exposed to interception and harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks by quantum-capable adversaries. This paper presents PQ-FL-IDS, a post-quantum (PQ) FL-IDS scheme for 6G edge networks. It protects model-update exchange using a real, non-simulated Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM-512, NIST FIPS 203), the Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode with a 256-bit key (AES-256-GCM), and per-round forward secrecy through ephemeral key pairs. Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) with Rényi DP accounting further bounds record-level leakage from local updates. In each round, clients train locally with calibrated DP noise, encrypt the model update, and send only the protected payload for server-side aggregation. We evaluate PQ-FL-IDS on ToN-IoT with a 1D-CNN and FedAvg, and on CICIoT2023 with MobileNetV2-1D and FedProx, under baseline, PQC-only, and PQC+DP settings. ML-KEM-512 with AES-256-GCM adds less than 0.003% computational overhead relative to per-round training time and at most 3.5 KB of payload expansion, with no accuracy loss, and remains stable from 2 to 5 clients. The privacy analysis shows predictable ε growth with the subsampling rate and characterizes the privacy-utility frontier: formal budgets of ε = 0.9-2.4 are obtained for σ = 0.8-1.1, with a utility cost that depends strongly on task complexity.

title: Semantic Low-Code Data Fusion on the Edge to Support Intelligent Traffic Management
abstract: Intelligent traffic management applications require integrating data from diverse sources on the road infrastructure like radar sensors, cameras, and connected vehicles. The growing computational power deployed on the edge enables distributed computation of the data and near-real-time traffic control. However, interoperability is hindered by two key challenges: heterogeneous protocols for data access and inconsistent data semantics across sources. A data harmonisation solution is needed to retrieve data from different data sources while enabling a uniform representation of the information for data fusion and integrated analysis. The paper describes our solution to support the low-code definition of data integration pipelines by configuring a set of modular and reusable components. We leverage Semantic Web technologies and declarative mapping rules to resolve semantic inconsistency through a common conceptual model. A set of deployment templates enables the execution of the pipelines both on the cloud or on the edge to support diverse downstream applications with different performance and scalability requirements. Finally, the paper discusses the testing and validation of such a solution to support the reduction of collisions caused by unsafe braking at road intersections in a live deployment at the Mobility Lab in Helsinki.

title: Constrained Diffusion from Binary Evaluations via Learned Doob h-Functions
abstract: Conditional generation under constraints that can only be checked on a finished sample, such as a molecular property filter, remains challenging for diffusion models: most guidance methods require differentiable measurement operators, paired conditional data, or rollouts of the base model at every step. We present a framework grounded in the Doob $h$-transform that reduces conditional generation to learning a single function, the probability that a noisy sample denoises into the constraint set. We learn this function from binary clean-sample evaluations alone, by squared-error regression on forward-noised labels; the base model is frozen, one lightweight head is trained per constraint, and noisy-state classifier guidance arises as a special case. The exact guidance step fades where the constraint signal provably vanishes and carries a factor of the inverse probability across samples, which normalized guidance discards: with the schedule and mean step size held fixed, equalizing the step costs 17.0 to 18.5 points of constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10 at comparable FID, across independently trained estimators. Guidance is more than 50$\times$ cheaper per satisfying sample than rejection sampling at a 1.7% base rate, raises a Lipinski-type property filter on QM9 from 54.3% to 96.8%, and lifts satisfaction on Stable Diffusion 1.5 from 7.2% to 60.0% at one sixteenth of the cost of derivative-free selection, which reaches 9.0%. These results demonstrate that binary evaluations of clean samples are sufficient supervision for constrained generation across pixel, latent, and molecular diffusion.

title: OnCache: Learning Dynamic Caching Schedules for Efficient Diffusion Inference
abstract: Diffusion models have revolutionized generative tasks but incur high inference latency due to iterative denoising. Cache-based strategies accelerate inference by reusing intermediate features, yet they largely rely on static, sample-agnostic schedules. Our empirical analysis reveals two factors that these schedules overlook. (i) denoising dynamics and computational requirements vary across prompts, motivating adaptive computation allocation. (ii) sensitivity to caching errors varies across timesteps, so static schedules may reuse features at error-sensitive steps or waste computation at less sensitive ones. We therefore propose OnCache, a dynamic caching framework that makes prompt-adaptive decisions online about how much computation to allocate and when to refresh cached features. A policy is trained offline on paired compute and cache continuations from identical denoising states, using differences in terminal fidelity and the number of function evaluations (NFE) to account for the downstream consequences of each decision. To further improve the generation quality, a neural corrector compensates for caching-induced errors and mitigates their accumulation throughout the denoising trajectory. Both components are lightweight and introduce negligible additional inference latency. On FLUX.1-dev, OnCache achieves a nearly $3\times$ generation speedup at $1024^2$ resolution, with LPIPS of $0.156$ and SSIM of $0.860$. We further extend OnCache to video generation on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency--quality trade-offs across both modalities.

title: Fuzzy e-Means: Fuzzy c-Means on Large Data with Moving-Average Mini-Batch Updates
abstract: Fuzzy c-means (FCM) gives every point a degree of membership in every cluster. Its standard solver, alternating optimization (AO), needs a full pass over the data per iteration and often many iterations, while methods built for large data stop at a worse objective or still need tens of passes. We run FCM with the optimizer of e-means, a recent mini-batch k-means that keeps moving averages of the number and the sum of the points in each cluster and sets its batch size and step size by scaling laws. The optimizer carries over because an FCM centroid is also a weighted sum divided by a total weight, but this direct transfer fails in two ways: the e-means rule that relocates nearly empty clusters also removes the centroids of small, distant groups, and FCM started from random points can settle in poor local minima. Fuzzy e-means (e-FCM) therefore starts with one pass of e-means with hard assignments and then runs fuzzy moving-average passes without relocation. On 28 configurations with up to 109.5 million points and 16,384 clusters, e-FCM reaches the objective of 25 AO iterations in two to four passes when clusters hold several hundred points or more, 11 to 20 times faster than AO on one-million-point embedding sets with 1,024 clusters. It ends within 0.16% of converged AO on these sets and below converged AO where AO from random points lands in poor minima, but it is slower than AO on small low-dimensional problems, where an AO pass takes milliseconds. Finally, the common fuzzifier m=2 makes the centroids collapse or merge on most high-dimensional sets, and e-FCM can choose the fuzzifier by matching a known overlap at about two passes per candidate value.

title: Time to Protection in Federated Intrusion Detection on Jetson Orin Nano Clusters
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) allows IoT devices to improve a shared intrusion detector without exchanging raw data. A device, however, can only learn from attacks that reach it, and because federated detection is evaluated as a whole for the fleet of IoT devices or averaged over attack classes, it is not reported how long a device that has never observed an attack class remains exposed to it without protection. The aim of this paper is to measure that exposure window, round by round, and to determine how it depends on the share of the fleet that already holds the class. We deployed a federated system with nine clients on two Jetson Orin Nano clusters connected over a WAN. As the main dataset, we used N-BaIoT, which covers two devices that were never infected by the mirai attack. It was tested with one to seven attacked clients and validated on CWRU and PAMAP2 datasets. The results showed that new class arrival depends on the share of the fleet that already knows about it, reaching 0.827 on mirai after one round when trained from the start with mirai data on seven out of nine clients, and reaching protection thresholds after 4, 17, and 39 rounds for seven, three, and two of nine clients attacked, when the model was initially trained without knowledge of mirai. Our findings show that federation delivers recognition of an attack class quickly when much of the fleet already holds it, and slowly or not within our horizon when only a few devices have been hit, which is the case a defender is most concerned with.

title: Re-identification Risks and Privacy Challenges in Connected Vehicle Systems
abstract: CEDR’s Trusted Integrity and Authenticity for Road Applications (TIARA) project equips National Road Authorities with the tools and insights needed to develop secure and privacy-preserving data infrastructures for Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems. In this paper we examine the privacy risks associated with C-ITS data, highlighting vulnerabilities in anonymisation methods and re-identification risks due to detailed data transmission, such as location and behavioural patterns. We explore state-of-the-art mitigation measures, including differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, and federated learning. We also emphasize the importance of frameworks like pseudonymisation, data minimisation, and transparent data sharing. Our findings reveal significant privacy risks in C-ITS data, including vulnerabilities in anonymisation, re-identification threats through detailed data transmission, and the potential for behavioural profiling and location tracking. This emphasises the need for advanced mitigation measures, robust regulatory frameworks, and collaborative efforts among stakeholders to ensure secure and privacy-preserving use of connected vehicle data. Finally, we propose systemic and regulatory recommendation to road authorities, and provide a timeline from strategy to deployment based on short-, to mid- and long-term solutions.

title: ComplexIF: A Challenging Multi-Turn, Multi-Constraint Instruction-Following Benchmark
abstract: As frontier LLMs saturate existing instruction-following benchmarks, measuring further progress requires harder tests that remain faithful to real use. In practice, users often combine several constraints, add them at different turns of a conversation, and expect all of them to hold in the assistant's response. We introduce ComplexIF, a challenging benchmark for this setting, together with the automatic pipeline that generates it. The pipeline expands seed requests into multi-turn conversations, weaves constraints into their turns, and keeps only tasks that a strong model can solve, so difficulty can be raised by adding constraints or turns while every task stays solvable. ComplexIF's two splits test complementary sides of instruction following: a verifiable split of format constraints, checked by programs, and a rubric split of semantic instructions, such as a tone or an audience, checked with an LLM judge. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, even the strongest satisfies every constraint on fewer than half of the verifiable tasks, and no model leads on both splits.

title: Neutron Imaging Enhancement for Lithium Batteries Based on Swin-Transformer and Image Fusion
abstract: Neutron imaging is highly sensitive to light elements such as lithium and is therefore valuable for non-destructive testing (NDT) and analyzing internal structural evolution in lithium batteries. However, limited neutron-source flux and detector performance often result in images with mixed noise, low contrast, and blurred edges, hindering accurate assessment of battery internal states. To address these issues, this paper proposes a lithium-battery neutron image enhancement method combining an improved Swin-Transformer with spatial-domain image fusion. First, an improved Swin-Transformer incorporating Multi-Dconv Head Transposed Attention (MDTA) and Global Response Normalization (GRN) extracts and reconstructs image features to suppress high-density white spots and Gaussian-Poisson mixed noise. Second, guided filtering and a gradient-adaptive mask are used for selective edge enhancement, while Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) improves local contrast. Finally, a spatial-frequency (SF)-based local block-weighted fusion mechanism adaptively combines the edge-enhanced and contrast-equalized images to preserve microscopic details while suppressing noise. Experiments show that, compared with BM3D, DnCNN, and GAN, the proposed method achieves strong performance in full-reference and no-reference evaluations. Its best PSNR and SSIM reach 33.0517 dB and 0.9637, respectively, while the NR-IQA and Natural Image Quality Evaluator (NIQE) scores are as low as 0.1794 and 4.0974. The method reduces artifacts and over smoothing, improving the visual fidelity and structural identifiability of lithium-battery neutron images.

title: Less Federation, More Personalization: One-Shot Multi-View Clustering for Federated Fall Detection
abstract: Federated learning is a natural fit for sensor-based fall detection, where data are privacy-sensitive and highly non-IID across subjects. A two-stage framework is proposed in which each client first learns label-free representations using FMMVCC, a multi-view clustering encoder that combines reconstruction, cross-view consistency, contrastive learning, and prototype-based objectives. The resulting encoders are then aggregated via a single round of FedAvg into a shared frozen feature extractor, decoupling representation learning from downstream classification. Experiments are conducted on the FallTL dataset, a wearable sensing benchmark evaluated under both binary (Fall/ADL) and 16-class (activity × Fall/ADL) granularities. Results show that FMMVCC achieves strong representation quality, outperforming four self-supervised baselines in binary classification (84.15% ACC) and providing competitive performance in the fine-grained setting. On top of these representations, the personalized closed-form classifier consistently outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, and shared analytic baselines by 8-13pp, and matches or exceeds FedProto in the 16-class setting while requiring no communication during inference. Finally, cross-client alignment metrics are shown to be weak predictors of downstream performance, while class-separability measures correlate more reliably with accuracy.

evidence.title: Less Federation, More Personalization: One-Shot Multi-View Clustering for Federated Fall Detection
evidence.abstract: Federated learning is a natural fit for sensor-based fall detection, where data are privacy-sensitive and highly non-IID across subjects. A two-stage framework is proposed in which each client first learns label-free representations using FMMVCC, a multi-view clustering encoder that combines reconstruction, cross-view consistency, contrastive learning, and prototype-based objectives. The resulting encoders are then aggregated via a single round of FedAvg into a shared frozen feature extractor, decoupling representation learning from downstream classification. Experiments are conducted on the FallTL dataset, a wearable sensing benchmark evaluated under both binary (Fall/ADL) and 16-class (activity × Fall/ADL) granularities. Results show that FMMVCC achieves strong representation quality, outperforming four self-supervised baselines in binary classification (84.15% ACC) and providing competitive performance in the fine-grained setting. On top of these representations, the personalized closed-form classifier consistently outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, and shared analytic baselines by 8-13pp, and matches or exceeds FedProto in the 16-class setting while requiring no communication during inference. Finally, cross-client alignment metrics are shown to be weak predictors of downstream performance, while class-separability measures correlate more reliably with accuracy.

title: S1Arena-MM: Which Multimodal Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
abstract: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. Which multimodal decisions can System-1 models handle, and where do MLLMs perform better? We introduce S1Arena-MM, a benchmark that gives every model the same decision requests and scores the probabilities it returns. It contains 51,060 questions across 94 tasks with image, video, and audio input, drawn from 94 public datasets and three program-generated ones. It also includes 102 closed-loop game environments that a model plays from screenshots; in real-time mode, the game continues while the model decides. We evaluate 33 open models: 12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs read at the answer token. On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM by 4.9 percentage points on images and is within one point of it on video and audio. Post-training for decisions mainly improves the probabilities: on video, a System-1 model has a lower Brier score than the MLLM that it is post-trained from in 10 of 12 pairs. With up to 2,048 thought tokens per question, the most accurate MLLMs pass the best System-1 models only slightly, and thinking raises the Brier score of most MLLMs. Closed loops separate the models: three System-1 models built on a 27B MLLM reach 22.0-33.3% progression in BALROG, and no other model exceeds 9.7% with thinking off. In real-time GameWorld, latencies of up to 1.1 s per decision cause no measurable loss of progress for System-1 models. Code and data: https://github.com/zhaoyang02/S1Arena-MM.

title: Separating Action Allocation from Image Matching in Visual Token Routing
abstract: Adaptive visual token routers aim to save computation while preserving the image detail needed to answer each question. A higher average score could reflect better choices for individual images or more frequent use of high resolution on tasks that need it. We distinguish the two by keeping action counts fixed within each task and comparing the router's assignments with random pairings of the same actions and images. On equally weighted ChartQA and TextVQA, both Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B gain from matching but lose more from their action frequencies relative to a task table, with a 1.71-point gain and a 3.95-point loss on 7B. Exchanging the continuous resolutions chosen by the external selector CARES also lowers quality on 7B. When requests arrive with task labels, the table outscores the discrete router by 1.92 points and saves 31.76 ms per complete 7B request on average.

title: Complementary Geometry in Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Gaussian Splatting has achieved high visual quality in novel view synthesis, but the accuracy of its rendered geometry remains a challenge. In particular, the rendered depth is computed as an opacity-weighted average along each ray, which may not correspond to the actual scene surface. In this paper, we observe that depth predictions from different views of the same frozen Gaussian representation exhibit complementary errors, allowing us to improve novel-view geometry using information from other views without modifying the original representation. Based on this observation, we propose REVEAL, a general framework that selectively refines novel-view depth using complementary geometric information. Specifically, we first reproject depth predictions from source views to the target view and combine them using robust multi-view consensus. We then introduce a learned selection mechanism to determine whether the candidate depth is more accurate than the original prediction, based on the expected reduction in depth error. In addition, we introduce RIG, a real-world benchmark captured with synchronized RGB-D cameras, which provides ground-truth depth for evaluating both static and dynamic reconstruction models. Experiments on 6 Gaussian Splatting backbones across 3 benchmarks show that REVEAL consistently improves depth accuracy while maintaining comparable rendering quality.

title: Tamper-evident retrieval for medical RAG: code, results and evaluation data
abstract: Code, results and evaluation data for the article "Provenance Before Content: Tamper-Evident Retrieval Protects Medical Retrieval-Augmented Generation Against Knowledge-Base Poisoning" (M. Maroufi, S. Lamzabi, S. Ziti; submitted to IJACSA, 2026). The package contains the full Python pipeline (knowledge-base construction from PubMedQA, PoisonedRAG-style attacks, Merkle commitments with ML-DSA-65 ledger endorsements, evaluation of 3 open LLMs under 5 attacks and 7 defenses, scalability benchmark), every model answer, the summaries behind every table and figure, and timing data. See README.md for requirements and reproduction steps. Warning: data/poison.json contains synthetic, deliberately misleading medical passages written for this robustness evaluation only. They are false and must not be used as medical information or training data.

title: Continuous Passive Target Tracking over Intermittent and Narrow Sensing Beams in 6G Networks
abstract: 6G networks promise an advanced infrastructure for high-precision passive sensing and tracking, particularly in emerging sectors like Low-Altitude Economy (LAE) and Internet of Vehicles. However, realizing passive sensing in 6G remains challenging due to its unique signal characteristics, especially the extreme directionality of narrow beams and the intermittent availability of sensing resources, which are subordinated to the primary communication traffic. In this paper, we propose SPOT, a novel passive beam tracking framework that achieves continuous, high-precision tracking using only temporally sparse sensing slots. We employ an Interacting Multiple Model combined with an Extended Kalman Filter (IMM-EKF) to robustly predict non-linear target dynamics. We further develop a beam selection strategy that maximizes Fisher information gain to minimize tracking uncertainty, integrated with an opportunistic exploration mechanism to detect emerging targets. To reduce computation complexity, we introduce a lightweight approximation of the Posterior Cramér-Rao Lower Bound. Extensive evaluations using both simulations and real-world datasets demonstrate that SPOT significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving a detection rate near 100% and an average tracking error below 1 meter, even in multi-target scenarios with highly sparse temporal updates.

title: Into My Arms: Structured reinforcement learning for autonomous transport of objects and humans
abstract: Whole-body humanoid manipulation remains bottlenecked by high-dimensional state-action spaces, contact-rich environments, and long task horizons. This trilemma is a challenge that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods are yet to resolve reliably. We address it with three contributions that add just enough structure to guide exploration: Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE) for whole-body manipulation, Interaction Gated Transport (IGT) for sustained transport over long horizons, and a Hinted Object Path (HOP) that resolves collision and search complexity bottlenecks. Across all three, the policy remains free to discover its own manipulation strategy. The method generalises from rigid object to human transport. As a flagship demonstration, we show, to our knowledge, the first bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin by a humanoid robot completed with no human intervention during execution. In the domain of human transfer, we show that a single policy can adapt across substantial variations in body mass, size, and random force perturbations, all while training on a single GPU in under an hour. Our approach offers a pathway to fully RL-driven humanoid manipulation, enabling assistive robots that can help humans. Website: https://elle-miller.github.io/into_my_arms

title: Music Circuit: Trace and Control Style Dynamics in Large Music Generation Model
abstract: Musical style, a global attribute that functions throughout a whole piece, is a lever widely used by users in modern large music generation models. Yet how style is represented inside these models, and which components drive it, remains largely unexplored. In language models, circuit analysis traces a representation to a sparse sub-network of a few key components, namely attention heads and MLP neurons, and has been used successfully to explain and control global attributes such as emotion. In this work, we use circuit analysis to study the mechanisms behind musical style. Based on YuE2, we build a dataset that pairs the same lyrics with five styles and design a three-step framework. First, stage localization shows that the style forms mainly in the score-planning stage. Second, static observation across the positions of this stage further reveals that style is not a fixed vector but a dynamic representation across tokens. Third, we therefore merge the activation differences across positions into one direction per style, and trace the neurons and attention heads that drive this direction into a sparse circuit. Without any style text, steering this circuit successfully transfers one piece into the target style, matching and even exceeding the style prompt. To our knowledge, this is the first work to analyze and control musical style at the circuit level in a large music generation model. Audio and score examples are available at https://aristo233.github.io/Music_Circuit/.

title: Why Adaptive Optimizers Struggle with Large Convolution Kernels
abstract: Large convolution kernels enlarge the receptive fields of ConvNets at a modest computational cost, but they are notoriously difficult to train. Existing large-kernel networks therefore rely on costly training techniques, such as parallel small-kernel branches with batch normalization. In this paper, we trace this difficulty to adaptive optimizers such as Adam, which normalize the update of every weight separately. Since input features rarely average to zero, all weights of a kernel share a common gradient, and these optimizers move the mean of a $k\times k$ kernel $k$ times as far as a single parameter. We find this mean amplification in widely used ConvNets and vision transformers, and show that it can force the maximal learning rate to fall as $1/k^2$. We further prove that the basis of the discrete cosine transform (DCT) isolates the mean and is the only orthonormal basis that diagonalizes every stationary gradient statistic with mirrored boundaries. We therefore train large kernels through their DCT coefficients and convert them back after training. The resulting method, DCT-Rep, requires only a few lines of code and adds no parameters, no inference cost and negligible training overhead. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation and image restoration show that DCT-Rep consistently improves large-kernel ConvNets and vision transformers, by $+0.79\%$ top-1 accuracy for a large-kernel ConvNeXt-T and $+0.43\%$ for ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K, $+1.4$ box AP on COCO, $+1.2$ mIoU on ADE20K and up to $+0.4$ dB on image deblurring, where the gain grows with the kernel size.

title: FrozenSFL: Model-Frozen Split Federated Learning for Resource-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning over Heterogeneous Edge Devices
abstract: Collaborative fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) at the network edge enables privacy-preserving and personalized generative intelligence, but is constrained by the limited memory and compute resources of edge devices. Traditional approaches, such as split federated learning (SFL), partition models between devices and a server, requiring iterative exchanges of activations/gradients while the server manages multiple submodels. This leads to substantial communication overhead, high activation storage costs, and severe server-side memory pressure when scaling to massive heterogeneous devices. In this paper, we propose FrozenSFL, a resource-efficient SFL framework for collaborative fine-tuning of LLMs across heterogeneous edge devices. At its core, FrozenSFL strictly freezes device-side submodels to eliminate both deviceside backpropagation and server-to-device gradient transmission, thereby removing on-device activation storage requirements and downlink communication overhead. Building upon this design, we improve the framework in two aspects. First, we design a layerwise LoRA aggregation strategy to handle structural heterogeneity introduced by device-specific model partitioning and enable efficient server-side updates. Second, we introduce a server-side feature caching mechanism that reuses invariant features, allowing subsequent training epochs to proceed offline and reducing redundant computation and communication. We implement the FrozenSFL system as an asynchronous multi-threaded pipeline, which serves as our real-world testbed for evaluation. On the device side, forward computation and data transmission are decoupled via a producer-consumer mechanism. On the server side, a first-in-first-out scheduling strategy serializes fine-tuning tasks across devices. A hybrid memory-disk streaming mechanism further buffers incoming data and ensures stable training under network variability. Extensive evaluations with representative models, including BERT-Base (0.11B), ViT-Large (0.3B), and LLaMA-2-7B (7B), validate the effectiveness of FrozenSFL. In particular, for LLaMA-2-7B, FrozenSFL can reduce device/server VRAM footprint by up to 14%/82.7% with only 1% accuracy loss, while achieving up to 6.7× fine-tuning speedup.

title: Open, Distributed Research Ecosystems for Intelligent Transport Innovation in Europe
abstract: Modern transport systems increasingly rely on complex, heterogeneous datasets to inform research, planning, and policy. However, centralized approaches to data storage and analysis face significant challenges: they compromise data sovereignty, increase transfer costs, and often limit reproducibility due to privacy and ownership constraints. Recent advances in federated models offer a paradigm shift, allowing algorithms to travel to the data rather than the reverse. This approach supports privacy-preserving processing while aligning with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles of scientific data management. Within this architectural philosophy, the RAISE project has implemented a Mobility Pilot to explore the application of federated infrastructures in the transport domain. The pilot operates across three distributed computational nodes hosted by research institutions in Belgium, Spain, and Greece, applying federated analytic workflows to electric vehicle telemetry data. Analyses are executed locally on distributed nodes, validating a scalable, secure alternative to centralized analytics. Results demonstrate the feasibility of federated models in mobility research, offering insights into EV energy efficiency while ensuring reproducibility and data sovereignty. The study illustrates the potential of open, distributed research ecosystems to drive intelligent transport innovation across Europe.

title: When Simpler Beats Learned: Dual-Weighted Sampling vs. Machine Learning for the Pricing Subproblem in Graph Coloring
abstract: The graph coloring problem can be solved to optimality by branch-and-price (B&P), but its performance hinges on the column generation (CG) step, where each iteration requires solving a maximum weight independent set (MWIS) pricing problem. The state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) pricing heuristic follows a prediction-sampling paradigm: a learned model scores each vertex of a graph, and independent sets are sampled from the induced distribution. We observe, however, that the scoring procedure does not need to be learned, and critically assess the role of ML by replacing the learned scores with the dual solution of the restricted master problem, resulting in Dual-Weighted Sampling, a proposed lightweight alternative that requires no feature engineering or training. Within a unified CG and B&P framework that varies only the pricing oracle, Dual-Weighted Sampling outperforms MLPH, hand-crafted heuristics, and exact solvers on the established graph coloring benchmark in both runtime and solution quality. In particular, it remains competitive on the DIMACS random family, where MLPH was shown strongest in the original evaluation, while achieving more than a two-fold speedup in CG runtime on recursive-sparse and real-world graph families.

title: GraphSeer: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Relational Image Retrieval with MLLMs
abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) store entities with photos and names and link them by facts. MMKG methods predict links between known entity IDs, and image retrievers, from CLIP to MLLM embedders, return entities that look like a query photo or match its description. Neither answers a common question about a new photo: which graph entity is related to the one shown, such as the team of a pictured player or the city of a landmark. We call this knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR): given a photo and a natural-language relation, retrieve the related MMKG entity, which rarely resembles the photo, whether the depicted entity is in the graph (known) or not (unseen). We build three benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata and in-the-wild OVEN photos. The task hides two hops: recognising which graph entity is shown, and recalling what it is connected to. GraphSeer bridges them inside one multimodal LLM: it links the photo to the graph, reads the facts of the best match, and retrieves with the hidden state at which the model is about to say the answer. An unseen entity has no facts of its own, but every candidate answer does, so a listwise verifier reads the other end of the graph: it re-ranks the top candidates by their facts and photos in one forward pass, and the facts matter far more than the photos. With Qwen3.5-27B, GraphSeer improves MRR on known entities by 24.2-70.0% over an MLLM embedder fine-tuned on the same data with the same budget. When it also fuses and verifies the embedder's candidates, it improves MRR on unseen entities by 12.5-25.6%, and on known entities it beats KG-completion models given the ground-truth entity ID.

evidence.title: GraphSeer: Multimodal Knowledge Graph Relational Image Retrieval with MLLMs
evidence.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) store entities with photos and names and link them by facts. MMKG methods predict links between known entity IDs, and image retrievers, from CLIP to MLLM embedders, return entities that look like a query photo or match its description. Neither answers a common question about a new photo: which graph entity is related to the one shown, such as the team of a pictured player or the city of a landmark. We call this knowledge graph relational image retrieval (KRIR): given a photo and a natural-language relation, retrieve the related MMKG entity, which rarely resembles the photo, whether the depicted entity is in the graph (known) or not (unseen). We build three benchmarks from YAGO, Wikidata and in-the-wild OVEN photos. The task hides two hops: recognising which graph entity is shown, and recalling what it is connected to. GraphSeer bridges them inside one multimodal LLM: it links the photo to the graph, reads the facts of the best match, and retrieves with the hidden state at which the model is about to say the answer. An unseen entity has no facts of its own, but every candidate answer does, so a listwise verifier reads the other end of the graph: it re-ranks the top candidates by their facts and photos in one forward pass, and the facts matter far more than the photos. With Qwen3.5-27B, GraphSeer improves MRR on known entities by 24.2-70.0% over an MLLM embedder fine-tuned on the same data with the same budget. When it also fuses and verifies the embedder's candidates, it improves MRR on unseen entities by 12.5-25.6%, and on known entities it beats KG-completion models given the ground-truth entity ID.

title: Demo: Multimodal Stress Monitoring with Split Federated Fine-Tuning on Mobile Devices
abstract: We present an end-to-end mobile system for proactive stress monitoring from wearable signals. The framework is supported by an extensible split federated learning system that enables on-device LoRA fine-tuning of large language models. By analyzing physiological data, the application distinguishes emotional states, summarizes recent trends, and provides brief, actionable suggestions. Upon detecting a negative emotional state, the paired smartwatch or smartphone proactively delivers notifications to users to encourage mindfulness. The on-site demonstration will showcase real-time sensing-inference on smartwatch-phone pairs, alongside a recorded split federated learning process that continuously learns from user private data. Our code has been open-sourced at: https://github.com/HKU-WILL-Lab/Multimodal-Stress-Monitoring-with-Split-Federated-Fine-Tuning-on-Mobile-Devices.

title: Estimating a Transition Point from Gibbs and Ground States
abstract: We study how observed many-body system size affects the number of state copies needed to estimate a zero-temperature first-order transition point. The unknown Hamiltonian has bounded, translation-invariant on-site and nearest-neighbour interactions on a 3D cubic lattice with local dimension three. The field coupling is known, and all models share a known boundary field penalizing one local level. The limiting order parameter is uniformly separated across the transition. Each query returns an independently prepared Gibbs or ground state at an adaptive field and system size. For error $ε$ and fixed confidence, we prove an exponential separation between two size caps at the same temperature. There are absolute constants $0<c_0<C$ and $c_1>0$ such that, at inverse temperature $β=c_1/ε$, restricting side lengths to $L\le c_0/ε$ requires $\exp(Ω(1/ε))$ copies in worst-case expectation, even with collective measurements. Allowing $L\le C/ε$ permits $O(\log^2(1/ε))$ copies and $O(ε^{-3})$ total spins, using local measurements and polynomial classical postprocessing. The minimax expected total spin count is $Θ(ε^{-3})$ uniformly for $β\ge c_1/ε$. At fixed positive temperature it is $Θ_β(ε^{-2})$, attained from one- and eight-site Gibbs states followed by exponential classical computation. For ground-state copies it is $Θ(ε^{-3})$. The lower bound uses a three-state ferromagnet whose boundary suppresses the sector carrying transition information. A spanning-forest argument and edge-boundary counting control its Gibbs weight uniformly over fields and allowed sizes, and a trace-distance hybrid argument handles adaptive learners with quantum memory. The upper bound combines finite-volume free-energy estimates, concavity and local order-parameter measurements.

title: RSWP: Robust SO(3)-Equivariant Watermarking for Panoramic Images
abstract: Robust watermarking for panoramic imagery is impeded by the topological mismatch between spherical signals and planar representations. Conventional methods fail under $SO(3)$ viewing rotations due to non-linear geometric warping and struggle with viewport extraction, which typically necessitates computationally expensive inverse remapping. To address these challenges, we propose RSWP, a watermarking framework grounded in icosahedral group theory. Leveraging the property that the icosahedral group ($\mathcal{I}_{60}$) serves as the largest discrete subgroup of $SO(3)$, we decompose spherical rotations into tractable local planar rotations and combinatorial facet permutations. Accordingly, we introduce a decoupling architecture that embeds watermarks into discrete facets and a theoretically guaranteed Equivariance-to-Invariance decoding paradigm. By employing an equivariant feature extractor followed by a permutation-invariant sorting module, this paradigm rigorously synchronizes rotation-distorted features. Moreover, the dual-extractor design inherently supports direct, blind watermark retrieval from partial 2D renderings without geometric calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSWP achieves state-of-the-art robustness against continuous $SO(3)$ rotations and viewport transformations while preserving high visual fidelity.

title: IteraSong: LLM-Guided Iterative Symbolic Music Creation in a Web DAW
abstract: Music creation is inherently iterative, yet many symbolic generation systems still center on producing or regenerating isolated outputs. We present IteraSong, an interactive web-based Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) for LLM-guided iterative symbolic music creation. Unlike one-shot generation systems, IteraSong supports a generate-audition-edit-refine loop over a persistent multi-track project. Users initialize a fully labeled pop draft, then progressively refine it through natural-language instructions. The LLM maps requests to a hierarchical action space of editing primitives exposed via Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, spanning global, track, section, and bar/note scopes. The demo enables attendees to edit multi-track compositions in natural language, apply deterministic and generative edits, and undo/redo changes in real time.

title: Modal-Organizational Theory of Artificial Intelligence (MOTAI): Visual Atlas of Cognitive Organization, Capability Spaces, and Organizational Transformations
abstract: MOTAI Visual Atlas: Cognitive Organization, Capability Spaces, and Organizational Transformations This visual atlas provides a systematic graphical representation of the Modal-Organizational Theory of Artificial Intelligence (MOTAI), a conceptual and formal framework for investigating artificial intelligence through cognitive organization, functional capabilities, compositional structures, resource constraints, and organizational transformations. The atlas contains 17 pages of scientific diagrams, conceptual maps, comparative tables, and explanatory visualizations. It illustrates the central relationships between computational implementation, causal-functional organization, accessible cognitive operations, and the transformation of possibility spaces. Main components: The conceptual architecture and analytical levels of MOTAI. The formal organization of cognitive states, operators, admissible compositions, constraints, and resource costs. The distinction between actualized, operationally accessible, and transformationally accessible cognitive capabilities. Compositional closure and resource-bounded capability spaces. Four forms of cognitive and organizational transformation. Functional equivalence, capability comparison, and organizational incomparability. Seven formal properties and their conceptual implications. The relationship between structural organization, cognitive novelty, and changes in accessible capabilities. The visualizations are intended to support theoretical research in artificial intelligence, cognitive science, philosophy of computation, causal abstraction, and the study of complex intelligent systems. Scientific status: This atlas is a theoretical and conceptual resource. It does not present experimental findings or claim empirical validation. Its diagrams represent formal definitions, illustrative examples, and philosophical relationships rather than experimentally established neural mechanisms. Contents: A 17-page vector-based PDF visual atlas and a ZIP archive containing PNG versions of the atlas pages. Related research: The atlas accompanies the foundational MOTAI treatise and its independent formal model specification. Version: 1.0 (November 2026). Research framework: EMPIRAXIS Research.

title: mmPoison: Targeted Clean-label Poisoning Attacks on mmWave-based Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Nowadays, mmWave-based human activity recognition (HAR) systems are widely used in smart homes, healthcare monitoring, and telemedicine. To achieve high accuracy, HAR systems require large-scale data collection from distributed sources for model training, such as edge devices or public repositories, which opens up opportunities for attackers to inject poisoned data into the training process, inducing false predictions and damaging the reliability of mmWave-based HAR systems. This paper presents targeted clean-label poisoning attack strategies, mmPoison, which injects imperceptible poisoned data into the training datasets for causing misclassifications on target instances in mmWave-based HAR systems without controlling the labeling process. In mmPoison, different attack methodologies are proposed for different attacker capabilities. For white-box setting, discriminative region masking is used to limit perturbations in discriminative regions. Then, mmPoison updates perturbations based on parameter trajectory alignment, and optimizes the poisoned instances to remain close to the clean instances. This process is iteratively applied to generate poisoned datasets. For black-box setting, mmPoison trains surrogate models with pseudo-label supervision and then uses them in a generator-discriminator framework to generate poisoned instances by jointly optimizing attack effectiveness and imperceptibility. Experiments conducted on public and self-collected datasets validate the effectiveness and imperceptibility of mmPoison in causing misclassifications within mmWave-based HAR systems.

title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.

title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.

title: Curvature Mismatch and Local Errors in Galaxy Property Estimation
abstract: Linear probes are widely used to evaluate learned representations and infer physical quantities from unlabelled data. The probe's predictions are from an affine function in ambient space restricted to the underlying representation, and consequently, even a representation that has complete information needed to predict a target can produce systematic probe errors when that information is encoded in a form inaccessible to the linear probe. Here we share that some of this probing error is due to the innate geometry of the manifold. Linear probes, when evaluated on a curved manifold, generally have a nonzero intrinsic Hessian (what we colloquially call "probe-facing curvature") given by $\langle w_N,\mathrm{II}\rangle$, the manifold's second fundamental form dotted with the probe's normal component. We fit linear probes to galaxy embeddings from five pretrained encoders and intervene on this curvature term to evaluate its contribution to the probe performance. We find that keeping this inherited curvature improves the local fit where it matches the label's curvature. Removing the curvature component of the probe where it does not match the label curvature also provides improvements, and correcting it in every neighbourhood raises held-out local $R^2$ by 0.006 to 0.010 on galaxies, gaining more where the two curvatures disagree. We isolated these gains to be from the underlying geometry and not an automatic guarantee from least squares training.

title: The AI Forecast Registry
abstract: An append-only registry by Satoshi Yamauchi (Japanese title: 予測の名簿) of public forecasts about AI. Each row records the statement verbatim in its original language, with the sentence before and after, the date and the primary URL; describes the form of the forecast (the presence or absence of a deadline, a subject, a magnitude and a resolution condition) independently of whether it proves true; and fills the outcome only with what the forecaster later said about their own forecast and what a primary source states as fact. No verdict by the recorder appears. Registration and outcome are recorded as separate PGP-signed commits, so that a third party can verify that a forecast was registered before its outcome was known. Only the author writes to the registry; every forecast that meets the admission criteria is admitted, whether it warns of danger, argues for safety or denies that a capability is near. The registry begins on 22 March 2023 with the Future of Life Institute's open letter "Pause Giant AI Experiments." Rows are never rewritten: outcomes are appended to the canonical data as separate records. The canonical data is data/registry.json; data/registry.csv (rows as registered) and data/outcomes.csv (appended outcomes) are generated from it. Japanese and English editions. This archived version (v1.1, 22 November 2026) holds 23 rows (5 recorded after resolution, 18 before) and is the first version archived after an outcome was appended to a row registered before resolution: row 009, whose deadline was the week of 21 to 27 September 2026. The registry is updated roughly once a month, and a new version is archived in each month in which an outcome is appended. AIをめぐる公開の予測を記録する、山内怜史による追記専用の台帳。各行は、発言を原文の言語のまま直前・直後の一文とともに逐語で記録し、発言日と一次URLを付す。予測の形(期限・対象・尺度・決着条件の有無)は、予測が当たるかどうかとは独立に記述する。帰結には、予測者本人が後から自分の予測について述べた言葉と、一次資料に記載された事実だけを置き、記録者の判定は書かない。登録と帰結は別々の署名付きコミットで記録し、予測が帰結より前に登録されたことを第三者が検証できる。台帳に書くのは著者一人であり、収載基準を満たす予測は、危険を警告するものも、安全を主張するものも、能力の到来を否定するものも、同じ基準で載せる。起点は2023年3月22日のFuture of Life Institute公開書簡「Pause Giant AI Experiments」。行は書き換えず、帰結は正本に別の記録として追記する。正本は data/registry.json で、data/registry.csv(登録時の行)と data/outcomes.csv(帰結の追記)はそこから生成する。日本語版・英語版を収録。この版(v1.1、2026年11月22日)は23行(決着後に登録5行・決着前に登録18行)で、決着前に登録した行に帰結を追記した後の最初の保存版である(009、期限は2026年9月21日から27日の週)。台帳は月に1回程度更新し、帰結を追記した月ごとに新しい版を保存する。

title: Sánchez, Feijóo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
abstract: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, Sánchez, Feijóo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for Sánchez and Feijóo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare Sánchez and right personas spare Feijóo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.

title: MoR4Rec: Mixture-of-Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.

title: Ego-HMB: Human Motion Bridging from Egocentric Images via A Motion Bridge Diffusion Model
abstract: We introduce Egocentric Human Motion Bridging, a task that generates a coherent 3D human motion sequence from two endpoint egocentric images. Unlike conventional motion in-betweening, which requires structured 3D endpoint poses, this setting uses raw first-person observations available from wearable devices in VR/AR and robotics. It presents challenges due to viewpoint variations, partial body visibility, and temporal ambiguity under cross-modal endpoint constraints. To address these challenges, we propose Ego-HMB, a unified diffusion-based framework that learns endpoint pose estimation and temporally consistent motion infilling within a single model through two training stages. First, Egocentric-to-Canonical Pretraining uses a hierarchical curriculum with progressively increasing temporal spans to strengthen endpoint pose priors. Second, Motion Bridge Diffusion Training incorporates endpoint and physics awareness, diffusing from neighboring poses to promote temporal continuity while preserving global endpoint constraints. Extensive experiments compare our approach with one-stage methods that directly generate motion from two egocentric images and two-stage pipelines that combine endpoint pose estimation with motion interpolation. Ego-HMB consistently outperforms these baselines in endpoint accuracy and motion generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/gaogehan/Ego-HMB.

title: MODAL-ORGANIZATIONAL THEORY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
abstract: One of the fundamental problems in contemporary artificial intelligence research concerns the relationship between the computational structures of intelligent systems and the cognitive capabilities they exhibit. Although artificial neural networks are typically described in terms of computational units, parameters, architectures, internal representations, and information-processing mechanisms, these descriptions do not fully resolve the conceptual distinction between operations currently performed by a system, operations that remain accessible under specified conditions, and transformations that may alter the system's repertoire of possible cognitive activities.This treatise develops a modal-organizational framework for analyzing artificial intelligence through the structure of its functional possibilities, the constraints governing their realization, and the transformations through which these possibilities may change.The central argument is that the organization of an intelligent artificial system cannot be adequately characterized solely by its currently realized computations. A broader analysis must also account for the relations between available operations, the conditions governing their composition, the resources required for their realization, and the permissible transformations of the organizational structures themselves.The proposed framework distinguishes five analytical levels: physical implementation, computational structure, causal-functional organization, compositional organization, and the modal structure of cognitive capabilities.A formal model of cognitive organization is introduced in terms of states, operators, composition rules, organizational constraints, and resource costs. On this basis, three categories of cognitive possibility are distinguished: actualized, operationally accessible, and transformationally accessible capabilities.The treatise further differentiates four types of organizational change: behavioral variation, compositional expansion, organizational-rule reconfiguration, and representational-space transformation.Four elementary formal propositions are developed concerning the invariance of capabilities under structure-preserving recoding, the insufficiency of restricted behavioral equivalence for establishing modal equivalence, the conservativity of adding an already definable operator, and the dependence of resource-bounded capabilities on implementation costs.The framework is examined in relation to causal abstraction, mechanistic explanation, functionalism, multiple realizability, computational mechanics, category-theoretic compositionality, dynamical systems, and theories of transformational creativity.A central conclusion is that novelty of output, novelty of capability, novelty of mechanism, and novelty of organizational principle must be treated as conceptually distinct phenomena.The proposed theory does not claim to establish a new physical constituent of intelligence or an empirically verified universal mechanism. Its contribution is a systematic philosophical and formal framework for examining the relationship between computational realization, organizational structure, functional possibility, and transformations of the space of accessible cognitive operations.

title: Selecting Stable Sampling Dynamics for Compositional Diffusion: A Feynman-Kac Weight Reduction
abstract: Given $K$ separately trained diffusion models, how should one sample from a $β_k$-weighted product of their terminal laws without jointly retraining the experts? Existing Feynman--Kac constructions provide many weighted stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with the correct target marginal. The consequential question is how to select useful proposal dynamics among them. We study an explicit family of weighted diffusions that realizes the same product-of-intermediate-experts trajectory. A scalar parameter $λ$ controls how strongly the proposal drift follows the composed expert score, while an additional Langevin component can be varied independently. Writing $B=\sum_{k=1}^{K}β_k>0$, we identify the distinguished choice $λ=1/B$. At this value, the aggregate squared-score term in the instantaneous Feynman--Kac log-weight rate cancels exactly. For positive expert exponents, the remaining score-disagreement contribution is non-positive. We call this structural cancellation Feynman--Kac reduction. Under bounded-divergence assumptions, it yields an upper bound on the instantaneous unnormalized log-weight rate for all $λ\leq 1/B$. For linear diffusion protocols with compactly supported expert data, $λ=1/B$ yields two-sided bounds at every nonterminal time, for exponents of either sign. A corresponding result holds for a single expert under the same divergence assumption. In these two-sided settings, the selected value is unique within the specified family in a universal worst-case sense. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and molecular sampling compare the analytically predicted stability with actual sampling quality, including instances in which parameter choices different from $λ=1/B$ perform better empirically.

title: Fill in the Blanks: Non-Autoregressive Schema-Parallel Key Information Extraction with CTC Decoding
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) extract structured data from documents by generating the requested JSON one token at a time, so their sequential steps grow with the length of the answer. Yet in key information extraction (KIE) the schema already fixes the answer's structure: keys, nesting and lists are known before decoding, and only the values are unknown. We exploit this with a non-autoregressive extractor that writes the structure from the schema, sizes every list with a count pass, and predicts all values in parallel, in a fixed number of passes that does not grow with the document. Each value is decoded with connectionist temporal classification (CTC) in its own block of slots, so its length never has to be predicted, and a value that is still open after its block gets a larger token budget. Zero-shot on VAREX, CORD and FUNSD, our 4B extractor is 3.5$\times$ faster than the diffusion-VLM competition on average (up to 5.6$\times$) and more accurate, with 4--6 forward passes per document where block diffusion needs 12--74. The same extractor also drafts for speculative decoding with its own autoregressive base: it runs 8.3$\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding (up to 10.4$\times$) within 0.4 points of its accuracy, and 3.3$\times$ faster than speculative diffusion decoding while 13.0 points more accurate. We release the model and code.

title: NANO: Unifying Missingness and Input Uncertainty in Tabular Learning
abstract: Missing values are common in tabular data, yet current approaches to handling them often overlook two dimensions. First, an observed value may be uncertain, while a Not-Observed (N.O.) value may still have a reasonable estimate. Inputs should therefore span a continuous spectrum from no evidence to a fully trusted observation. Second, Not-Applicable (N.A.) means that no meaningful value exists for a record, yet this semantic state often lacks explicit representation. To address both dimensions, we introduce NANO, a unified plug-in for input encoding that fits most token-based architectures. Guided by Bayesian evidence weighting, NANO adjusts the influence of a supplied value according to confidence, with all zero-confidence estimates mapped to the same N.O. representation. NANO accepts, but does not require, per-example confidence information during training or inference. For N.A., a separate representation enables models to encode inapplicability and its schema-defined reasons into context. Experiments across eleven datasets and nine backbones show that mixed-confidence training enables a single NANO model to generalize across inference confidence levels, remaining competitive without estimates and improving steadily as estimate reliability and confidence increase. The effectiveness of NANO's handling of N.A. is further demonstrated on three augmented datasets.

title: Human-Centric Trustworthy AI: AITHENA’s Methodological Framework for CCAM and Key Insights
abstract: This paper presents AITHENA’s human-centric, trustworthy AI methodology tailored for Cooperative, Connected and Automated Mobility (CCAM) systems. Recognising that public trust is essential to the adoption of AI-powered mobility, the framework translates high-level ethical principles, i.e., fairness, transparency, accountability, and privacy, into a practical Trustworthy AI qualitative checklist for developers, operators, and regulators. By integrating empirical user research on user mobility needs, expectations, and concerns, the methodology offers concrete tools to address trust challenges regarding AI in CCAM. The paper details how user perspectives are mapped to actionable checklist items, outlines implementation guidance, and discusses policy pathways aligned with the EU AI Act and automotive safety standards. Ultimately, AITHENA aims to bridge the gap between ethical theory and real-world application, fostering AI-driven mobility systems that reflect societal values and regulatory requirements.

title: probly: Uncertainty-Aware Machine Learning
abstract: As machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the question of how to represent and quantify uncertainty has moved from a methodological side issue to a central concern. In practice, however, making a model uncertainty-aware is still surprisingly difficult: relevant tools tend to be scattered across libraries, each tied to a particular framework and a particular approach to modeling uncertainty, and the choice of representation, quantification, and evaluation is typically left to the user without much guidance. In this paper, we present probly, a Python package that addresses these issues in a single, modular framework. probly offers (i) lightweight transformations that turn existing models into uncertainty-aware ones, currently supporting PyTorch, scikit-learn, and Flax, (ii) several representations, including second-order distributions, credal sets, and conformal prediction, (iii) the corresponding quantification measures, and (iv) a number of evaluation protocols, which can be combined more or less arbitrarily. Using probly, we conduct a benchmark study on three standard tasks --- selective prediction, out-of-distribution detection, and active learning. In addition, and unlike existing benchmarks, we evaluate suitable methods on first-order data, i.e., datasets for which the target itself is a distribution over outcomes. We further illustrate the flexibility of the package on a number of less standard case studies, including large language models, graph neural networks, and data streams. The package is publicly available at https://github.com/pwhofman/probly.

title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

title: The Evaluation Substrate Matters: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Serving Substrates
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) usually coordinate heterogeneous models and tools to solve complex tasks, creating a growing need for reliable evaluation. However, a multi-agent workflow that is fastest in one serving environment can lose its advantage in another, even when its models, prompts, and task remain fixed. This makes a benchmark result conditional on how the workflow is executed. We introduce MASSys, a benchmark for measuring this dependence in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. MASSys executes the same candidate-task pairs across serving substrates and load regimes, using five workload families spanning software repair, research synthesis, financial analysis, interactive control, and diagram generation. It records task quality alongside delivery, latency, cost, resource pressure, and failure evidence. In a controlled motivation diagnostic, the Star workflow falls from first to fourth in mean-latency rank under KV-cache pressure, while Chain rises from fourth to first. The substrate sweeps further show that increasing load creates long runtime tails and timeout pressure. In several task families, quality among evaluated outputs changes less than effective quality over submitted jobs: the system delivers fewer usable results even when the surviving outputs remain competitive. Tool and runtime traces reveal that these outcomes involve both model serving and non-model execution. Together, the results motivate evaluating MAS designs over explicit operating conditions and reporting which tasks are delivered, how well they are solved, and where execution breaks down.

title: NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments
abstract: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.
