title: graspit-py: A Python Interface to GraspIt! for Grasp Planning Under Pose and Friction Uncertainty
abstract: In simulated multifingered grasps, pose error can change contacts formed during hand closure, while friction uncertainty changes the loads supported by those contacts. Existing C++ APIs and ROS 1 services provide programmatic GraspIt! access but require native bindings or a service transport layer for Python use and application-specific integration of contact geometry with uncertainty sampling. A Python workflow for these studies must connect native closure and contacts to caller-defined wrench scores, uncertainty samples, and command reconstruction. We present graspit-py, a Python interface to native GraspIt! operations that supplies this workflow. The interface provides native scene access, contact-wrench analysis, and configurable approach planning under pose and friction uncertainty. A grasp record associates the object-relative palm pose and closed independent coordinates with nominal contacts and quality scores evaluated under sampled pose and friction conditions. Our MuJoCo exporter derives serial hinge chains and affine joint couplings, including nonzero reference angles, and preserves individual collision components. Across 75 configurations of five hand models, maximum discrepancy between source and exported palm-frame vertex sets was approximately 1.3 micrometers against a 100-micrometer geometry tolerance. We isolated reference-angle and collision-component effects through controlled ablations and validated 1,920 directional task-wrench capacity calculations against independent Cartesian-force linear programs. In a common GraspIt! workload, median reset-close-score-state cycle latency through direct Python was 10.7% lower than through persistent ROS 1 services. An executable export-plan-reconstruct workflow and grasp examples on six hand models demonstrate how the contact, score, and joint representations support numerical analysis and command reconstruction.

title: Beyond the section plane: Robust 3D reconstruction of multiplex immunofluorescence exposes limitations of 2D spatial cell statistics
abstract: Spatial analysis of the tumour microenvironment with multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) typically relies on single thin tissue sections, which misrepresent the 3D tissue organisation and bias spatial cell statistics in ways that remain largely unquantified. We reconstruct 24 breast and lung tumour tissue microarray cores in 3D, each from 15-20 serial mIF sections, and compare spatial cell statistics in 3D with those from individual sections. Our pipeline combines affine pre-alignment with dense deformable refinement using RoMa v2, achieving a median target registration error of 1.79 $μ$m, well below nuclear size, which allows nuclei to be linked across sections. While cell-type proportions are preserved in 2D (Pearson corr. $r \geq 0.99$), 3D analysis reveals up to 3.8 times shorter nearest-neighbour distances, 13-19% higher neighbourhood entropy, and 2-4 times more contacts per cell. Tissue composition can thus be reliably estimated from individual sections, whereas cell-cell interactions require volumetric analysis.

title: Improving the Improver: Semantic PID Control for Medical Agent Self-Improvement
abstract: High-stakes vertical medical tasks, such as postoperative pathological staging and long-term survival prediction, demand multi-step clinical reasoning over heterogeneous evidence under weak supervision and high outcome uncertainty. While we first orchestrate CliAgent, a domain-tailored clinical agent workflow that systematically grounds predictions in multi-modal patient evidence, manually designed medical agents remain constrained by static, brittle rules. Moreover, existing recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods suffer from feedback ambiguity and severe development-set overfitting when evolving agents in high-noise medical domains. Focusing on improving the improver, we propose Semantic PID-RSI, an evidence-guided control-theoretic framework for medical agent self-improvement. Inspired by PID control, our improver evaluates candidate modification batches via three diagnostic roles: P isolates current clinical failure modes, I synthesizes longitudinal evidence from past trials, and D estimates response dynamics and regression risks (D-pre/D-post). Selected plans are compiled into behavior contracts for staged probing and independent adoption judging. Instantiated and validated on challenging oncology tasks (pT/pN staging and survival prognosis), evolving CliAgent with Semantic PID-RSI on a 3B-activated open-weight model achieves substantial gains (up to +6.27 C-index points), outperforming overfitting-prone RSI baselines and approaching the performance of frontier proprietary models (e.g., GPT-6 series) equipped with CliAgent.

title: Decoding Frozen Vision Representations for Training-Free Few-Shot Pineapple Detection
abstract: Few-shot object detection in agricultural imagery is hampered by dense vegetation, repeated patterns, and scarce annotations. We present a training-free detector that turns dense features from frozen visual foundation models directly into detections, without fine-tuning, a learned head, or external proposals: a whitened foreground-background direction estimated from annotated support images scores every query patch, and the score field is decoded with an adaptive threshold and support-derived geometry. We also test whether predicted relative depth can be fed directly to RGB-pretrained frozen encoders. On aerial pineapple imagery, the detector outperforms PET-DINO and GeCo2 at every evaluated support size; at K=40, predicted depth alone reaches 92% of the RGB performance with DINOv2, and RGB-depth fusion lowers counting error for both encoders. We release the Pineapple Plantation dataset (4,908 aerial frames, 1,995 annotated with 17,609 boxes, predicted depth, leakage-aware splits) and analyse transfer to two further agricultural datasets.

title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation
abstract: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.

title: ViewAgent3D: A Training-Free Multi-View Pipeline for 3D Scene Understanding
abstract: 3D scene understanding tasks are often approached by building explicit 3D scene representations or by training specialized multi-modal models over point clouds, voxels, or scene graphs. We take a complementary view: for many queries, the main bottleneck is not the absence of a stronger 3D representation but the selection of a small subset of multi-view RGB views that actually makes the query answerable. We present a training-free, query-conditioned multi-view pipeline that performs diverse tasks using only 2D images and a set of tools used purely for inference. Our method first decomposes each query into a set of concepts that identify unique attributes that assist with reasoning. This drives a coarse-to-fine evidence selection process: a coarse retrieval selects and scores all views, a diversity-aware selector reduces redundancy, and a reranking stage helps shortlist views by target visibility or answerability. The resulting evidence is optionally grounded for queries that benefit from explicit localization, and a self-verification step helps refine the final response, especially for open-ended cases. Despite using no task-specific training and no explicit 3D representations at inference time, our approach provides approximately 10% gain on 3D VQA and 5% gain on dense captioning and Embodied QA while being applicable across different scenarios. We further propose a unique judge-based evaluation system, motivating a judge who takes into account many semantically correct or partially correct answers, thereby improving holistic scene understanding.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Runbook Improvement with Agentic Support Automation
abstract: Operational support is an important component of production software services. Support requests are often emergent and can come in many forms such as customer escalations or unplanned service interruption. Engineers across organizations have been successful in implementing automation to help streamline support processes but many solutions remain in the hands of human operators. A successful strategy to improve operator response times is to maintain up-to-date runbooks which are documents enumerating triage steps and remediation procedures in the face of identified incidents. This paper is an investigation into an operational system which incorporates Agentic AI into a runbook based incident resolution pattern. The bot uses information in the runbook corpus along with some system-specific tooling to guide the manual operator through the mitigation process then evaluate the outcome and suggest edits to the runbook where it found gaps and in its ability to triage the situation. By using the runbook as a medium to bridge humans and automation, the process maintains explainability and can be decoupled from the agent system. This paper demonstrates a collaboration between human operators and Agentic AI with results from an 17 week study involving 232 production incidents. We conclude with lessons on integrating LLMs into DevOps workflows, related work in AI-assisted operations, and guidance for reproducibility.

title: Gaze Graphs: A Scene-Level Representation of Visual Attention in the Operating Room
abstract: Purpose: Analyzing clinicians' visual attention from exocentric camera views can support surgical scene understanding without requiring wearable eye trackers. However, existing gaze-following research in the operating room (OR) estimates only 2D gaze locations without identifying attended scene entities or localizing gaze targets in 3D space. In this work, we investigate gaze graphs as a scene-level representation of visual attention that connects clinicians to attended scene entities, and evaluate their utility for fine-grained surgical action recognition and semantic scene graph (SSG) generation. Methods: We extend the public EgoExOR dataset with gaze annotations to create EgoExOR-Gaze, the first benchmark for multi-view gaze graph generation in the OR. We propose a novel architecture that jointly estimates 3D gaze targets and predicts attended entities using only exocentric camera views. Specifically, our approach exploits 3D gaze geometry to sample local visual features across multiple views for attended entity prediction. We further utilize predicted gaze graphs for fine-grained surgical action recognition and SSG generation. Results: For gaze graph generation, our model outperforms both exocentric-only and combined exocentric-egocentric baselines. For surgical action recognition, our model incorporating predicted gaze graphs outperforms both exocentric and egocentric baselines across all evaluated metrics, with particularly strong gains in temporal metrics. For SSG generation, incorporating gaze graphs improves macro-F1 from 0.42 to 0.52 compared to exocentric inputs alone, although performance remains below that achieved with egocentric inputs. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate the value of gaze graphs for surgical action recognition and SSG generation, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling scene-level visual attention even when egocentric views are unavailable.

title: PFN-Syn: Generating Synthetic Tabular Data with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
abstract: Synthetic tabular data can help enable data sharing and model development in privacy-sensitive domains, but existing generators often require dataset-specific training and substantial computation. We introduce PFN-Syn, a training-free framework for synthetic tabular data generation based on prior-data fitted networks. We evaluate PFN-Syn against training-based generators on eight binary classification datasets. PFN-Syn achieves the highest average downstream utility among evaluated synthetic generators, with higher generation throughput than training-based baselines, while maintaining competitive distributional similarity and distance-to-closest-record privacy behavior. Our results suggest that tabular foundation models can serve as useful building blocks for practical synthetic tabular data generation.

Our results suggest that tabular foundation models can serve as useful building blocks for practical synthetic tabular data generation.

title: Learning Continuous Scene Depth Representations via Cross-Modal Gaussian Rendering
abstract: Depth super-resolution with color guidance is a fundamental problem in geometric scene understanding that aims to reconstruct high-resolution depth using structural cues from color images. In practical RGB-D systems, the resolution gap between depth and color images often varies, requiring flexible upsampling factors. However, many existing methods are designed for predefined integer scales. Although implicit methods support arbitrary-scale reconstruction, they typically rely on computationally demanding per-pixel neural decoding and may struggle to recover sharp depth boundaries and fine structures. To this end, we propose a cross-modal Gaussian rendering framework that learns continuous depth representations for arbitrary-scale depth super-resolution. Specifically, we first construct hierarchical Gaussian representations for progressive depth reconstruction, with explicit spatial support defined by learnable Gaussian primitives. Building on this representation, we design a Structure-Aware Gaussian Aggregation module that combines spatial weights with cross-modal feature affinities to reduce aggregation across depth discontinuities. We then develop a Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Rendering module that adapts Gaussian spatial kernels to the target pixel footprint. To further facilitate cross-modal learning, we propose a training strategy that gradually introduces higher-frequency guidance information during training. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method at both in-distribution and out-of-distribution upsampling scales.

title: Lean Census: A Distributional Analysis of AI-Generated Lean Code
abstract: We compare two human-written and four AI-generated Lean libraries with Mathlib through the distributions of simple statistics of their code. For each library we measure inline claims in proofs, proof length, how often each declaration is used, and design choices such as instances and private declarations, and we read each against the variation among Mathlib's own areas. The AI-generated libraries have more inline claims per theorem, longer proofs, fewer instances, and more private declarations than the human-written ones. We release the code for the analysis as a package, lean-census, at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census.

title: Topological Neural Collapse
abstract: Neural collapse (NC) predicts that, late in training, last-layer class features concentrate at their means and the means form a simplex equiangular tight frame (ETF). We ask whether NC also leaves a signature in the functional connectome of each layer: the graph of Pearson correlations between hidden-unit activations, built per class and summarized by persistent graph homology. Using deep MLPs, we observe two topological phenomena that co-occur with the well-studied geometric NC in the final layers during the terminal phase. Contrary to NC1, the split-half variability of a class connectome increases (TNC1). The mean pairwise $H_0$ distance $\bar{D}$ between class connectomes also rises (TNC2), but unevenly across class pairs, unlike the equidistance of NC2. We find that 24-56% of last-layer units become dead for some classes yet stay active for others, which inflates $\bar{D}$. After correcting for these units, both signatures remain elevated. These results from MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 provide preliminary evidence that a topological mechanism may accompany the geometric signatures of NC.

title: Controlled One-Click Benchmarking and Post-Fusion Recalibration for Support-Conditioned Medical Segmentation
abstract: Sparse-prompt medical segmentation is hard to compare when prompts, supports, thresholds, and splits differ. This paper uses a controlled one-click protocol: each test image receives one positive foreground click, training-only support, validation-only checkpoint selection, and no test-time threshold tuning. We propose {Support-Aware Recalibration (SAR)}, a late post-fusion recalibration block for MultiverSeg that combines large-kernel spatial gating with squeeze-and-excitation channel recalibration after support--query fusion. BUSI, NerveUS-BP-present, and Kvasir-SEG are evaluated with matched 697 foreground-present sample budgets, shared splits/clicks, and threshold-free Dice-AUC/IoU-AUC. Compared with a protocol-matched raw-support MultiverSeg baseline, the main SAR configuration shows favorable mean Dice-AUC/IoU-AUC performance on BUSI, NerveUS-BP-present, and Kvasir-SEG, while reducing logged training time in this implementation. These controlled results indicate that late post-fusion recalibration is useful under a leakage-controlled one-click protocol.

title: FormaFin: Verifiable Financial Analysis with Solver-Guided Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Formally verifying financial analyses generated by large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as financial rules are largely expressed in natural language and rarely have corresponding formal specifications. Training language models to formalize these rules is hindered by the scarcity of labeled data and reliable training signals, while confidential financial data favor small models that run locally. We introduce FormaFin, a framework that trains small open language models to translate financial rules into reusable SMT formulas. FormaFin integrates teacher distillation with reinforcement learning using an SMT solver to compute rewards from numerical thresholds stated in financial rules. We evaluate FormaFin on corporate loan monitoring, in which lenders check borrowers' financial figures against loan agreements. To evaluate our framework, we curate \bench{}, a benchmark containing 143 loan agreements and 2,527 questions covering compliance, earnings cushion, and debt capacity. Our results show that a 7B formalizer achieves 94.8\% accuracy, outperforming open LLMs up to ten times larger. Across three model families, accuracy ranges from 92.6 to 96.8\%. Our framework also detects 95.6 to 99.7\% of errors in other LLMs' financial analyses. We make FormaFin and \bench{} publicly available.

title: A Novel Approach to Clustering Shape Data Using Iteratively Weighted Vectors with k-Means
abstract: Topological data analysis provides a collection of methods for analyzing data with shape structure, including point clouds, graphs, and images. Recent advances in topological vectorization have enabled the embedding of shape data into Euclidean spaces, facilitating comparisons and machine learning tasks. Vector summaries that effectively capture topological structures are particularly useful for shape classification and unsupervised learning tasks such as clustering. We investigate the use of vectorized topological data for clustering through k-means, which partitions observations into a fixed number of groups by minimizing a squared-error loss function. By incorporating an element-wise weight-update step into the iterative k-means algorithm, we improve clustering performance on both simulated and real-world shape datasets. We show that estimating these weights reduces to a least-squares problem, requiring minimal additional computation while allowing flexible coefficient constraints. Our approach also substantially strengthens the negative correlation between the loss and clustering accuracy, improving the effectiveness of selecting among multiple clustering solutions based on the lowest loss. These improvements remain robust to changes in vector length and the number of initializations. Furthermore, weighted topological vector summaries exhibit stability under small structural perturbations, particularly when weight constraints are imposed. The proposed method offers a flexible alternative for clustering topological data, accommodating different k-means variants, vectorization methods, and weight constraints.

title: DeRail: Escaping Trajectory Priors via Counterfactual Action Steering for Mid-Execution Instruction Switching
abstract: Robots operating in the real world must often adapt when user instructions change mid-execution, yet current instruction-conditioned robot policies, including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), are largely evaluated under fixed-instruction episodes. We study mid-execution instruction switching and identify trajectory hijacking as a key failure mode, where the policy fails to redirect sufficiently toward the switched target, with its post-switch behavior remaining fully or partially drawn toward trajectories associated with non-target tasks. We propose Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS), a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that identifies interfering non-target tasks, queries the same policy with corresponding counterfactual instructions, and uses target--counterfactual action differences to steer execution away from interfering trajectory priors. Experiments on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch across five VLA and WAM policies, together with real-robot evaluation, show that CAS consistently improves switching success; for example, on CALVIN-Custom-Switch in the [15,21] switching range, CAS improves π_{0.5} from 5.8\% to 54.6\%. Successful CAS-guided rollouts further provide higher-quality self-training supervision than vanilla successful rollouts with the same number of trajectories, yielding stronger policies that generalize to unseen later instruction switches. Code will be made publicly available.

title: Robust Forest-based Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Under High-dimensional Confounding
abstract: Understanding how patients with Alzheimer's disease respond differently to treatment is important for individualized therapeutic assessment. Using observational data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we investigate how the association between donepezil dosage and 12-month cognitive performance varies across diagnostic stages and hippocampal volumes. This analysis presents several statistical challenges, including potentially nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity, high-dimensional confounding, and heavy-tailed outcomes with extreme observations. To address these challenges, we develop an Orthogonal Huber Random Forest (OHRF) framework that combines Huber-based robust estimation, Neyman orthogonality, and forest-based adaptive weighting. The proposed method accommodates complex treatment effect heterogeneity while reducing sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors and extreme outcomes. We establish its consistency, asymptotic normality, and finite-sample error bounds. Simulation studies demonstrate favorable estimation accuracy and robustness across a range of error distributions, particularly under heavy-tailed noise and outlier contamination. In the ADNI application, OHRF produces generally narrower pointwise confidence intervals than the conventional Orthogonal Random Forest (ORF) while revealing distinct patterns of treatment effect heterogeneity across diagnostic groups and hippocampal volumes. These findings illustrate the potential of robust, data-adaptive methods for studying heterogeneous treatment responses in complex observational biomedical data.

title: Eidetic Code World Model
abstract: Executable code can preserve a world's structural layout, yet video renderers frequently alter the appearance of previously visited places once they leave the camera view. We present Paintress, a code-conditioned world model that couples an executable geometric proxy with an independently parameterized 3D Gaussian appearance memory in a shared metric coordinate frame. While the proxy enforces structural and visibility constraints, 3D Gaussians capture the visual realization synthesized by emitted observations. To balance stable incremental fusion with consistent readout, Paintress separates writing from reading: newly emitted frames update a persistent raw Gaussian map under confidence-gated selection, whereas a cloned reader copy is globally refined against the observation archive and rendered with coverage masks to condition generation. We also introduce Expedition-33, a benchmark for generated-appearance retention across 11 static scenes, five route families, and 15, 30, and 60 s target absences (165 settings per system). Excluded from the opening image, targets are synthesized during a shared prefix and scored against each system's own first visit at matched return cameras. Across ten systems (1,650 videos), Paintress achieves 0.1220 ROI-LPIPS, 0.0613 MAE, and 52.12% detail retention (vs. 0.2731, 0.1401, and 10.91% for CWM), with lower discrepancy at 60 s (0.1630) than CWM, AgentGarten, and Lyra 2.0 achieve at 15 s.

title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

title: Correlation-aware sequential sampling for multi-output polynomial chaos expansions
abstract: The interaction of multiple physical processes in complex engineering systems is often characterized by several quantities of interest (QoIs) with non-negligible cross-correlations. Accurate uncertainty quantification of these responses requires repeated model evaluations, which can be computationally expensive. As an alternative, polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) provides an efficient surrogate modeling framework for reducing this computational cost owing to its natural structure for statistical analysis, while adaptive sequential sampling can further improve sampling efficiency under a limited model evaluation budget. However, adaptive sampling strategies specifically designed for multi-output PCE remain limited, and existing approaches commonly aggregate information from individual outputs without explicitly accounting for their statistical dependence. When strong correlations exist among QoIs, output-wise aggregation can give greater combined influence to response patterns shared by several outputs. To reduce the influence of such repeated representation on sample allocation, this study develops a principal component analysis-based extension of the multi-output criterion for adaptive construction of PCE. The sampling criterion combines component-wise normalization with the retention of selected principal directions, thereby adjusting the relative influence of shared response patterns while preserving distance-based exploration. The method is verified through numerical examples with different levels of output coupling and is compared with the conventional multi-output criterion and reference sampling strategies. The results demonstrate that accounting for output dependence improves the allocation of new samples among multiple response features and enhances the efficiency of multi-output PCE surrogate construction, particularly for strongly correlated QoIs.

title: Dual-Stream Event-to-Video Reconstruction
abstract: Event cameras capture brightness changes with high temporal resolution and dynamic range, but converting event streams into videos remains fundamentally ill-posed due to the lack of absolute intensity information. Resolving this ambiguity calls for a brightness reference that complements the intensity changes recorded by events. Inspired by the complementary spatial and temporal processing of the parvocellular and magnocellular pathways in human vision, we propose EvDualDiff, a dual-stream framework that combines a brightness reference from temporal-mapping events with motion-event cues for video reconstruction. Conditioned on both streams, our video diffusion model autoregressively reconstructs long sequences from a single temporal map. Photometric constraints and finetuning on self-generated rollouts reduce accumulated drift. At the hardware level, our approach requires only a minimal light-modulation mechanism on the lens of an event camera. We build this setup and collect a dataset comprising temporal-mapping events, motion events and synchronised ground-truth RGB frames. Experiments on a public benchmark and on our collected EvDual dataset demonstrate that EvDualDiff outperforms existing event-to-video reconstruction methods in fidelity, perceptual quality and video-level realism. The code and dataset will be released.

title: Beyond Invoice Volumes: Temporal Network Structure, Maturity Concentration, and Systemic Liquidity Exposure in SME Trade-Credit Networks
abstract: Trade-credit invoices encode directed obligations whose temporal synchronization and counterparty concentration are obscured by annual volume totals. We audit 749,952 atomic B2B invoices from 2012-2023 (EUR 99.705B; 75,343 firms) from the pseudonymized Mendeley Data corpus (Esteva de la Rosa, 2026), separating 1,240 terminal 2024 bridge records (EUR 630.12M; 9 bridge-only firms) and 13 extreme-duration contracts (>3,650 days; EUR 297.75k). Using directed weighted graphs, HHI, Shannon entropy, CR1 shares, spectral centralities, and multi-cadence temporal operators, we formulate and benchmark a Maturity-Aware Network Exposure (MANE) indicator. Invoice values are heavily skewed: the top 1% hold 81.41% of value (Gini = 0.9742). Two-way fixed-effects panels with circular block bootstrapping ($B=999$, 12-month blocks) and Holm-Bonferroni control show higher lagged debtor counterparty concentration is associated with lower MANE ($\hatβ=-0.494$, 95% CI $[-0.752,-0.248]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.004$). Robustness audits (R1-R4) confirm stability under 2021 exclusion ($-0.402$, $p=0.004$), Shannon entropy ($+0.257$), CR1 ($-0.515$), 1%-99% Winsorization ($-0.462$, all $p=0.001$), and multi-invoice debtors (count $\ge 2$, $-0.334$, $p=0.031$). Conversely, within-FE diagnostics expose severe joint-concentration multicollinearity (VIF = 22.22) that vanishes for multi-invoice debtors ($p=0.719$), while regime splits reveal a macro reciprocity sign reversal between 2012-2019 ($-0.706$) and 2020-2023 ($+0.232$, both $p=0.001$). In 12-month purged forecasting, MANE does not reliably improve over maturity seeds ($Δ\mathrm{MSE}=2.668$, 95% CI $[-0.027,7.954]$; trimmed $0.067$, $[-0.035,0.194]$), positioning MANE as a reproducible screening and auditing diagnostic, rather than a default proxy, for supply-chain finance, multilateral clearing, and RWA tokenization.

Robustness audits (R1-R4) confirm stability under 2021 exclusion ($-0.402$, $p=0.004$), Shannon entropy ($+0.257$), CR1 ($-0.515$), 1%-99% Winsorization ($-0.462$, all $p=0.001$), and multi-invoice debtors (count $\ge 2$, $-0.334$, $p=0.031$). Conversely, within-FE diagnostics expose severe joint-concentration multicollinearity (VIF = 22.22) that vanishes for multi-invoice debtors ($p=0.719$), while regime splits reveal a macro reciprocity sign reversal between 2012-2019 ($-0.706$) and 2020-2023 ($+0.232$, both $p=0.001$). In 12-month purged forecasting, MANE does not reliably improve over maturity seeds ($Δ\mathrm{MSE}=2.668$, 95% CI $[-0.027,7.954]$; trimmed $0.067$, $[-0.035,0.194]$), positioning MANE as a reproducible screening and auditing diagnostic, rather than a default proxy, for supply-chain finance, multilateral clearing, and RWA tokenization.

title: UACR: Uncertainty-Aware Collaborative Routing for Explainable Industrial Anomaly Inspection
abstract: Industrial anomaly inspection requires not only accurate anomaly discrimination but also trustworthy explanations for operators, while satisfying the strict latency constraints of online inspection. Existing methods, however, typically apply a fixed computational path to all samples, making it difficult to strike a good balance among detection accuracy, inference efficiency, and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose UACR, an uncertainty-aware collaborative routing framework for explainable industrial anomaly inspection. UACR aims to deliver reliable anomaly decisions together with operator-facing explanations under the online inspection budget, while adaptively allocating computation so that ambiguous cases receive deeper scrutiny. The framework consists of two stages. Stage I, Offline Training and Routing Hyperparameter Search, learns the anomaly inspection modules and calibrates the uncertainty estimator that drives routing. Stage II, Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Routing, collaboratively dispatches each input across inspection paths according to its estimated uncertainty. Experimental results on multiple public datasets show that UACR achieves over 5.16% improvement in accuracy compared to the baseline method, while reducing latency by over 31.5%. It also enhances the interpretability of industrial detection by over 15%.

title: Stein Guidance without Gradients: Discretization Uniform Diffusion Inference Time Scaling beyond Particle SMC
abstract: Reward-guided diffusion requires effective steering and correction of the bias introduced by approximate value functions. A Brownian example shows that SMC with full multinomial resampling at every step can require particle counts to grow linearly with guidance depth to maintain accuracy. We propose Stein Guidance, which combines derivative-free guidance with whole-path independence Metropolis-Hastings correction. Value-weighted selection from centered Gaussian candidates approximates gradient guidance in expectation, using as few as two queries per step. Centering stabilizes the local normalizer estimates, and the same queries yield an explicit path weight for correction. Under uniform value and spatial regularity bounds, we prove superpolynomial decay of finite-grid total variation error in the number of MH updates, with constants that do not grow with guidance depth. The error prefactor tends to zero as the value functions approach exact Doob values and the time grid is refined.

title: SENSA: Visual-to-Brain Generation with Individualized Subject-State Transfer and Adaptation
abstract: Visual-to-brain encoding predicts neural responses to visual stimuli, supporting visual cognition research and neural decoding. However, challenges in disentangling shared from image-specific activity, together with inter-subject distribution shifts and representational heterogeneity, limit accurate encoding and cross-subject generalization with limited calibration data. We introduce SENSA, a structured continuous neural response generation framework that separates shared activity from image-dependent responses and calibrates a compact subject state. An independent response prior captures shared activity, while complementary visual descriptors drive separable sensor-time bases and a shared Response Refiner. Subject-Adaptive Factor Transport adjusts the spatiotemporal expression of shared bases, while Source-Grounded Residual Memory predicts image-dependent corrections in source-response coordinates. Together, they personalize a frozen generator using limited paired support. Experiments demonstrate that the generation backbone outperforms recent generators across three datasets, with image-identity perturbations confirming stimulus specificity. Using only 400 paired images, electroencephalography (EEG) and the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) calibration achieve residual Pearson correlations of 0.1091 and 0.2995, respectively, demonstrating effective brain-response generation and cross-subject adaptation.

title: Unlearning Model Identity: Ablating LoRA Weights from Question-Based Identity Tuning
abstract: Large Language Models are trained on diverse corpora containing outputs from proprietary teacher models and provider-curated sources. Models subsequently inherit embedded self-identity traits, persistently asserting specific proprietary names. Service providers of open-weight models frequently require the removal of model identity for downstream applications, such as custom interfaces, without exposing provider affiliations to end-users. Effective identity modification is therefore critical for customized model alignment and deployment. This study proposes a method to localize parameter-level representations of self-identity within low-rank adaptation modules to perform targeted weight ablation. By generating probing questions designed to elicit self-naming outputs and fine-tuning the base model on these responses, the approach identifies and ablates high-magnitude weights within the parameter set. Experimental results demonstrate that distilled identity traits reside within a localized subset of low-rank weights, achieving a complete removal rate in Qwen3.5-2B and a 10% rate in Gemma4-E2B while preserving general task capabilities. These findings confirm that ablating top-tier adaptation weights suppresses distilled self-identification without compromising broader model performance.

title: KineState-SWAM: A Surgical World Action Model with Explicit Kinematics and Causal Interaction Dynamics
abstract: Existing surgical world models often leave implicit how instrument motion drives localized tissue responses and how interaction history informs subsequent actions. We introduce KineState-SWAM, a surgical world-action model coupling action prediction and video generation through a persistent interaction state, separating kinematically determined instrument motion from learned scene evolution. A flow-matching policy predicts joint trajectories conditioned on interaction state, robot configuration, and task instruction. Kinematic Geometry Conditioning converts these trajectories into surface-motion tokens and spatially aligned instrument renderings using calibrated URDF kinematics. Causal Interaction Dynamics recurrently updates the state through geometry-guided attention and motion-aligned feature transport, carrying interaction history into subsequent action predictions without intermediate video synthesis. The State-Geometry Adapter combines state-dependent spatial modulation with localized geometric residuals to guide video generation. Interaction-aware supervision emphasizes tissue responses near instrument working regions. We introduce dVRK-Chole5.2k, comprising 5,255 videos spanning 17 surgical tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines within matched action-conditioning settings. Ablations support preserving and transporting interaction states for long-horizon prediction.

title: Thakaa at StanceEval-2026: Inference-Time Target Grounding for Arabic Stance Detection
abstract: StanceEval-2026 tests Arabic stance classification under target shift, with evaluation targets absent from the labelled task data. We test two ways to supply target information at inference time. For Track 1, we retrieve eight labelled Women Driving demonstrations from the external ArabicStanceX corpus and score the three label tokens with Gemma-4-31B-IT. For the unseen-target track, we prepend cached target context prompted to be factual and non-evaluative, then fuse label predictions and label-token scores from multiple LLMs, with final assignments constrained by published class totals. The systems obtain 85.22 and 91.78 Favg2 on Tracks 1 and 2, ranking sixth and fourth in the final standings. On held-out ArabicStanceX tweets, direct prompting scores 79.45 Favg2; eight random Women Driving demonstrations raise it to 84.78, and similarity retrieval reaches 89.04. Across three target-held-out Mawqif evaluations, a fixed target card raises Gemma-4-31B-IT from 86.54 to 86.93, whereas QLoRA lowers Gemma-4-12B-IT from 84.43 to 83.77. In these separate public evaluations, same-target demonstrations and retrieval improve performance, factual target context provides small, target-dependent gains, and the tested source-only adapter does not improve.

title: Beyond Full-Context Accuracy: Context-Marginalized Evaluation of Test-Time Structure-Aware Inference in EEG-to-Image Retrieval
abstract: Test-time structure-aware inference can improve cross-subject EEG-to-image retrieval by exploiting relations among unlabeled test queries, but it also makes predictions depend on query-set composition. Existing evaluations typically report accuracy under a single full-query context, leaving unclear whether gains and comparative conclusions hold as context changes. We introduce Context-Marginalized Retrieval Evaluation (CMRE), which repeatedly evaluates each target query in sampled contexts using the corresponding rows of a fixed query-gallery similarity matrix. CMRE distinguishes structural exploitability, quantified by gains over independent retrieval, from context robustness, measured by same-query Top-1 context consistency. Under leave-one-subject-out evaluation on THINGS-EEG2 across six frozen representations and six structure-aware inference rules, structure-aware inference improves full-context Top-1 accuracy by up to 20.40 percentage points over independent retrieval. However, the rule selected under full-context evaluation is no longer optimal in 17 of 24 representation-context-size conditions (70.8%). Selecting the full-context winner incurs an average loss of 2.70 percentage points and a maximum loss of 8.29 percentage points under reduced contexts. Representation rankings are likewise inference- and context-dependent: the ordering under independent retrieval is not consistently preserved under structure-aware inference. Moreover, larger retrieval gains do not necessarily imply greater context robustness, showing that retrieval effectiveness and prediction stability provide complementary views of structure-aware inference. Full-context accuracy captures one operating point of context-dependent inference. CMRE complements it by characterizing how structural gains, context consistency, and comparisons of rules and representations change with query context.

title: Identity in the Age of AI: Toward a Functional Postphenomenology
abstract: Advanced AI systems increasingly mediate the cognitive and practical functions through which personal identity is enacted: intention formation, deliberation, memory, self-expression, preference formation, and relational interaction. Drawing on Western and Confucian conceptions of identity, this paper advances a functional hypothesis specifying six domains in which AI may be reorganizing the conditions of agency, and outlines the implications for responsibility, consent, dignity, and institutional design. The argument is functional and normative rather than metaphysical: not that agency disappears, but that the architecture of the self that is presupposed by our normative categories may require renewed examination.

title: Interaction Retention and Output-Likelihood Training in Parallel Sampling
abstract: Parallel samplers such as masked diffusion language models generate several coordinates per step from conditional marginals and randomize which coordinates are generated together, so even exact conditionals return a distorted distribution. We give an exact local account of this distortion. Around any full-support product law, the Gram operator of the sampler's response is diagonal in the interaction decomposition, and its eigenvalues are retention probabilities: the probability that an interaction has a unique latest-revealed coordinate. This retention spectrum determines the exact frontier between output accuracy and conditional calibration, its regularization path, and the population response of finite-mixture likelihood training. For pairwise interactions it yields a sharp dichotomy. Under homogeneous retention, output-likelihood training is equivalent to a single context gain; heterogeneous retention opens correction directions beyond any scalar, with an advantage bounded by an explicit heterogeneity gap. On binarized digits and MNIST, output-likelihood training within a heterogeneous schedule library lowers calibrated test negative log-likelihood in all twelve paired comparisons, and the gain survives pair-specific recalibration and a stronger path optimizer. For a frozen 169.6-million-parameter masked diffusion language model, serially normalized context gains are 1.070 and 1.056 at 8 and 16 rounds, against the predicted values 1.134 and 1.058.

title: OrthoLatentCAD: Orthographic Spatial Latents for Hand-Drawn CAD Program Generation
abstract: Freehand orthographic drawings capture early design intent, yet recovering executable sketch--extrude CAD programs from raster front, right, and top views remains challenging: noisy, dimension-free 2D layouts must be reconciled into an ordered construction history. We introduce Hand2CAD, a benchmark of 215K ABC-derived synthetic orthographic-drawing--CAD program pairs and 1,000 real three-view sets drawn by CAD-trained participants. Recovering CAD programs from orthographic drawings requires both cross-view geometric reasoning and alignment between visual features and program representations. We propose OrthoLatentCAD to address these two challenges. It fuses local geometry with global context on canonical planes, exchanges evidence between paired plane lines indexed by the same shared-axis coordinate, and maps the spatial representation to ordered program latents through queries inherited from a frozen CAD autoencoder. Across the evaluated one- to three-view configurations, OrthoLatentCAD outperforms protocol-matched baselines in procedural accuracy, compiled geometry, and CAD-kernel validity while benefiting from additional views. Without real-data fine-tuning, it also outperforms the baselines on held-out real drawings. We will release the dataset, code, and evaluation scripts.

title: Model choice and prompt framing in LLM sustainability judgments
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for sustainability assessment and decision support, yet their judgments may depend on the selected model and on how the task is defined. We compare 13 locally executed open-weight LLMs on 80 author-written sustainability scenarios using three prompt families that ask which actor should be responsible, bear the costs, or initiate action. Each model answered at two temperature settings with 100 repetitions, producing 624,000 deposited outputs, of which 610,708 contain a complete score vector. Scores were analyzed as relative actor support after removing each response’s overall level. Within this instrument, the cost prompt family produced the highest cross-model disagreement, exceeding both responsibility and catalyst by 7.37 points (question-cluster 95% intervals 5.56−9.15 and 5.38−9.36, describing variation across these 80 scenarios). It also produced the most lead-actor disagreement and the lowest full consensus. Moving from catalyst to cost reduced relative support for government and increased it for individuals and firms; moving from cost to responsibility largely reversed this pattern. These differences exceeded temperature-setting differences and persisted under model exclusion, alternative score transformations and tie rules, missing-response checks, and stems without explicit cost wording. Exploratory category patterns are conditional on uneven item coverage. Secondary rationale-language comparisons show the same within-model ordering but not the most cross-model variation under cost. Operational use should disclose model, prompt, and temperature choices; compare plausible alternatives; repeat generations; and refer high-disagreement judgments for human deliberation.

title: Thakaa at AlexandriaX-2026: Who Gets the Final Say? Assigning Output Authority in Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation and Error Detection
abstract: We report first-place systems for all four evaluated AlexandriaX-2026 settings: both English-to-dialect translation tracks, cross-dialect translation, and translation-error detection. In unconstrained translation, our minimum Bayes risk (MBR) selection restricts output authority: four local systems can supply the translation, while seven additional systems contribute only reference evidence. Candidate-constrained MBR beats the strongest complete candidate in all 13 dialects and gains 1.2554 macro spBLEU overall, reaching 33.4891. It also surpasses a retrospective oracle selecting the best whole candidate system per dialect. In the constrained track, country-routed LoRA adapters over a shared NileChat-3B-Base backbone incorporate the released Libyan and Sudanese supervision absent from the training and development splits, raising macro spBLEU from 29.5969 to 30.4233. Post-evaluation, a single adapter trained on all released Alexandria data reaches 30.4733 macro spBLEU; averaging model weights across three training seeds raises this to 30.9726 while retaining one model for inference. For cross-dialect translation, nonparallel target-dialect retrieval guides deliberation, raising Gemma-4-31B-IT without fine-tuning from 24.6898 to 28.4011 spBLEU. For translation-error detection, GPT-5.5 proposes semantic error regions, while MARBERTv2 controls their character boundaries and corroborates additional spans, raising Overall from 0.4691 to 0.4982.

title: Aegis: A Conversational Prototype for Lung Cancer Risk Information and Follow-up
abstract: Collecting self-reported risk information and maintaining continuity between assessment, explanation, and follow-up are practical components of a lung cancer screening workflow. We present Aegis, a browser-based research prototype that combines a conversational questionnaire, rule-based risk categorization, downloadable reports, retrieval-augmented health information, and doctor-user communication. A session-oriented controller manages question progression and clarification, while a language model assists with answer validation. Structured responses are passed to a separate risk-analysis module, and reports are linked to user and session records through Firebase services. The project adopts a multi-agent design that separates information collection, validation, assessment, and report generation. Its documented verification scope comprises 45 functional test specifications covering account management, questionnaire interaction, reporting, doctor-side review, and consultation. The available evaluation describes workflow behavior qualitatively; it provides no per-case execution results, clinical cohort, predictive-performance measurements, or comparative experiments. We therefore present Aegis as an engineering prototype for organizing risk information and follow-up, with clinical validity and the benefits of its agent-based design remaining unestablished. The paper describes the implementation, distinguishes implemented workflows from incomplete extensions, and identifies the evidence required for reproducible and clinically meaningful evaluation.

The paper describes the implementation, distinguishes implemented workflows from incomplete extensions, and identifies the evidence required for reproducible and clinically meaningful evaluation.

title: PhyMind: Physics-Informed Masked Autoencoding for EEG Foundation Models
abstract: EEG foundation models are pre-trained almost exclusively with masked reconstruction through a free-form decoder, sometimes with hand-crafted spectral targets added, as in MANAS-2. We study what happens when that decoder is replaced by a generative forward model of EEG. PhyMind keeps a standard masked transformer encoder, but its decoder must explain the masked signal through 68 cortical regions, each driven by damped stochastic oscillators and an aperiodic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, projected to the recording's own montage by a fixed boundary-element lead field evaluated per derivation. Training combines masked reconstruction with a Whittle spectral likelihood, an oscillator-dynamics residual, a minimum-norm source prior and a penalised neural residual. In a controlled comparison (same encoder, data, steps and seed), the physics decoder produces encoder tokens whose spectral content is far more linearly decodable than with a masked-autoencoder decoder or with the MANAS-2 objective: mean R^2 on a token-level spectral probe with amplitude-normalised targets is 0.67/0.77/0.77 on three datasets, against 0.24/0.50/0.50 (MAE) and 0.48/0.67/0.66 (MANAS-2 objective), approaching the released 92.8M-parameter MANAS-2 (0.71/0.81/0.80). Downstream gains in the controlled setting are small (four-task mean balanced accuracy 56.6 vs. 53.8 for MAE frozen, 63.8 vs. 62.7 fine-tuned). Region-level features from the physics decoder raise frozen four-class motor-imagery accuracy by 7-14 points, so a 7.2M-parameter model pre-trained on 3k hours of open EEG is comparable to the released MANAS-2 with frozen features (63.0 vs. 61.6). After full fine-tuning, MANAS-2 remains better (66.8 vs. 65.4 for our best model). The inferred sources do not reproduce the lateralisation that a classical inverse solution finds in motor imagery, so we do not claim anatomical interpretability. Code and weights are released.

title: CrossPanel: Exposing the Answer-Evidence Gap in Scientific Figure Understanding
abstract: A correct answer to a scientific-figure question can conceal an incorrect account of the experiment. Reading evidence across panels requires keeping each observation attached to the object and conditions that give it meaning. We introduce CrossPanel, a benchmark of 2,650 human-reviewed questions that exposes this answer-evidence gap. Its tasks combine parallel observations or follow dependent queries, while a response audit separates object selection, experimental conditions, cross-panel binding, and local readout. Across 15 vision-language models on 251 diagnostic questions, 8.42%-56.64% of correct answers contain explicit factual errors. The audit distinguishes coherent readings of the wrong target from incorrect readings of the right one. Controlled interventions then test how these failures can be repaired: verified object-condition hints, which withhold the requested measurement, raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's target-query success by 22.81 percentage points on 57 questions, while additional image tiles alone yield little improvement. Other models benefit most from combining both forms of assistance. These findings identify experimental attribution as a distinct requirement alongside local perception, and make both measurable beyond final-answer accuracy.

title: Dynamic Model Merging with Multi-Layer Aggregated Routing Evidence
abstract: Dynamic model merging aims to retain the efficiency of a unified model while better preserving task-specific expertise through input-dependent routing at both the task and head levels. However, even the routing components of the state-of-the-art approach remain limited: the task routing is highly sensitive to the choice of routing layer, whereas the head routing relies on simple max-logit competition. To address these limitations, we propose multi-layer aggregated routing evidence (MATE) as a unified mechanism for improving both task and head routing. Specifically, we first introduce a metric to quantify task routing separability across different layers. Empirical analysis of this metric reveals that different layers provide complementary evidence for identifying the tasks relevant to an input. Motivated by this observation, MATE selects multiple informative layers according to their routing separability and aggregates their layer-wise routing scores to produce a more robust signal that can be directly used for task selection. Moreover, we observe that this signal also encodes useful information about the suitability of the corresponding classification heads. This motivates us to further combine the MATE signal with the max-logit score to guide classification head selection. Extensive experiments on vision benchmarks demonstrate that MATE consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Mitigating Backdoors in Masked Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models because they can predict multiple tokens in parallel rather than generating tokens sequentially. However, recent studies have shown that MDLMs are vulnerable to backdoor attacks: when an input contains an attacker-chosen trigger, a backdoored model generates a targeted output, such as malicious code, while otherwise behaving normally. Despite this threat, backdoor defenses for MDLMs remain largely underexplored. We present UNMASK, the first defense framework for MDLMs that detects trigger-containing inputs, localizes the trigger tokens, and removes the backdoor from the compromised model. UNMASK exploits two fundamental properties of backdoor triggers, specificity and dominance, to assign a suspiciousness score to each input token. By leveraging two distinctive capabilities of MDLMs, parallel token prediction and token reconstruction at arbitrary positions, UNMASK computes these scores both effectively and efficiently. We further provide a theoretical analysis supporting the design of UNMASK. Evaluations across 40 settings spanning two attacks and four models show that UNMASK detects 99.3% of trigger-containing inputs at a 5% false-positive rate, substantially outperforming the strongest adapted baseline, which achieves 54.8%. UNMASK also achieves over 99% trigger-localization accuracy and reduces the average attack success rate from 95% to 1%, while largely preserving the model's utility on clean inputs.

title: Bias Cascade: Understanding the Gap Between Knowledge Alignment and Effect Replication in LLM-based Social Simulation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate participants in social experiments. Existing research has primarily focused on aligning social knowledge and isolated responses, while overlooking whether simulations can reproduce the collective effects of social interventions. This distinction is critical due to a failure mechanism we call a $bias$ $cascade$: similar individual states can lead to different actions, while agreement on isolated actions can still produce divergent outcomes through dynamic interactions. As a result, models may produce accurate social judgments yet fail to reproduce the outcomes of classic human studies. To investigate this problem empirically, we introduce $REFLEX$ (Reproducing Effects of Foundational Literature EXperiments), a benchmark of 30 counterfactual social experiments grounded in classic human studies that compares knowledge judgment with effect simulation. Knowledge judgment directly predicts the direction of an intervention's effect, whereas effect simulation fixes the scenario and participants while varying one prespecified social factor, with agents generating actions from local observations that are aggregated into macro-level average treatment effects. Compared with human-study findings, the best-performing model achieves net directional scores of 0.847 for knowledge judgment and 0.453 for effect simulation. Moreover, longer causal chains are associated with poorer effect replication, consistent with the bias-cascade hypothesis. These findings reveal a substantial gap between knowledge alignment and effect replication, showing that current LLMs remain inadequate for reliably simulating collective human behavior.

title: Make Position Uninformative: Exchangeable Self-Distillation Flattens the Lost-in-the-Middle Curve
abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models answer well when the relevant document comes first or last and poorly when it sits in the middle. Some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. We show how training contexts teach positional bias. With a uniform answer slot and shuffled distractors, the optimal reader ignores position. Building on this result, Exchangeable Self-Distillation (ExSD) trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to reproduce the model's answer when it reads the answer document alone. It needs no gold answers and only a few thousand examples. On six models from 1.5B to 32B parameters, ExSD raises both average and worst-position accuracy against the frozen model, including on a held-out test split. In controlled LoRA comparisons, it significantly improves both criteria over Pos2Distill. Against CORD, mean differences are not significant, while worst-position accuracy improves significantly in the 20- and 30-document settings. ExSD also matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning, changes behavior on other tasks far less, and transfers to unseen tasks. Head probes show greater reliance on content over position.

title: SemGuard: Semantics-Decoupled Watermarking for Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Gaussian Splatting provides an efficient representation for high-fidelity rendering of static and dynamic 3D scenes, motivating the copyright protection of Gaussian assets. In CLIP-guided Gaussian watermarking, a universal message decoder pretrained on textual watermark representations is subsequently applied to visual features containing both watermark information and scene-dependent semantics. However, text-only pretraining does not explicitly account for the semantic interference encountered during watermark extraction. To address this challenge, we propose SemGuard, a simple yet effective semantics-decoupled watermarking framework that learns to suppress scene-dependent semantic interference during universal message decoder pretraining. Specifically, SemGuard combines message-related CLIP text features with message-independent visual features extracted from unwatermarked scene images, constructing training representations with controllable semantic interference relevant to the target Gaussian assets. A progressive semantic interference curriculum gradually increases the contribution of visual features, allowing the decoder to first learn reliable message representations and then adapt to increasingly strong scene-dependent semantic interference. After pretraining for a given message length and semantic image pool, the decoder is frozen and reused across multiple Gaussian assets whose visual semantics are covered by the pretraining data. Experiments on static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting assets demonstrate improved rendering fidelity alongside reliable watermark extraction, while evaluations on static assets further show enhanced robustness against image-space distortions.

title: Weight-Space Backdoors in Open-Weight LLMs: Cross-Architecture Attacks and Blind Model Forensics
abstract: Open-weight language models are vulnerable to trigger-conditioned behaviors introduced through sparse post-training weight modifications, creating supply-chain risks beyond conventional provenance checks. We present Neural Sentinel, a cross-architecture study of gradient-guided backdoor insertion and model forensics spanning 18 checkpoints across 14 architecture families (124M-31.3B parameters), including state-space and recurrent models. On Phi-2, modifying approximately 0.0002% of parameters induced an exact short-marker output after 300 steps (332 seconds), with mean next-token KL divergence of 1.5 times 10^{-5} and 100% top-1 agreement over evaluated positions of eight fixed reference prompts. Separate experiments produced structured tool-call-formatted outputs without establishing downstream execution. We identify three procedure-dependent response regimes -- Gradient-Permeable, Scale-Threshold, and Gradient-Fragmented -- and evaluate PPO-based weight-space exploration, which showed no statistically significant advantage over random search. For defense, Neural Sentinel combines weight-difference analysis, trigger discovery, activation probing, and contextual output inspection. In a 22-artifact development cohort, its reference-optional scanner classified 4/5 backdoored artifacts as BACKDOORED; the remaining positive and all 17 clean artifacts were SUSPICIOUS. These findings establish the feasibility of sparse conditional-output insertion and evidence-producing forensic triage, while identifying limitations in behavioral-drift assessment and clean-model admission.

title: When Strong Reasoners Join the Pool: Small Union Premiums and Costly Runaway Generations in LLM Routing
abstract: Routing benchmarks often judge a router against a hindsight oracle that counts a query as solved whenever any model's recorded answer is correct, but under stochastic decoding that oracle mixes two different objects: the clairvoyant ceiling of committing to one model per query and the premium of calling several models and keeping any correct answer. A companion study measured this premium at 3.5 percentage points (pp) for 11 small open models on MATH-500; how large it is once current reasoning models enter the pool was unknown. We measure it with a fixed-protocol, pre-committed generation on a single NVIDIA B300: all 500 MATH-500 problems, 30 seeded samples per problem, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and NVIDIA's Nemotron Nano 9B v2 and Nemotron Super 49B v1.5 (a NAS derivative of the same 70B) under vendor sampling, a 65,536-token cap, a pinned Math-Verify scorer, and an append-only attempt ledger, for 45,000 scored responses. The two reasoning models both reach 96.1% accuracy against 76.2% for the 70B baseline. The empirical product-coupling premium is 0.215-0.588 pp across all two- and three-model pools; the empirical plug-in selection headroom over always calling Nano is 1.27 pp; and resampling Nano three times gives practically the same empirical any-correct rate as calling all three models once. Only 31 responses reached the cap, 25 of them with exactly periodic tails, yet the capped responses account for up to 60.2% of a model's output-length-squared proxy, and long generations made a fourth planned model, Llama-3.1-8B, too slow to finish. The premium is far below the companion's 3.5 pp, but models, pool size and protocol changed together; an oracle gap should therefore be reported with the pool, the protocol, the samples per cell and the decoding budget that produced it.

title: MQCODet: Modality Quality-Guided Collaborative Optimization for UAV-Based RGB-T Tiny Pedestrian Detection
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based RGB-thermal (RGB-T) remote sensing provides complementary visual and thermal information for pedestrian perception under complex aerial observation conditions. However, detecting tiny pedestrians in UAV-based RGB-T imagery remains challenging due to cross-modal spatial heterogeneity, manifested as modality quality imbalance and spatial position misalignment. Existing RGB-T detectors primarily address these challenges at the feature fusion stage, without establishing an effective coupling between feature fusion and object localization, potentially resulting in suboptimal detection performance. To address this limitation, we introduce a Modality Quality-Guided Collaborative Optimization Detector (MQCODet), which extends modality quality from a fusion prior to a localization supervision cue. Specifically, we propose a Dynamic Calibration and Region-Aware Fusion (DCRF) module that progressively refines cross-modal spatial alignment and performs region-aware fusion to generate reliable multi-scale features and a scene-level modality quality prior. We further design an Efficient Contextual Interaction (ECI) encoder to enhance multi-scale feature interaction while preserving fine-grained spatial details. Moreover, we propose a Modality-Aware Adaptive (MAA) loss that incorporates the modality prior and object scale to adaptively balance spatial consistency and geometric similarity for localization supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MQCODet surpasses state-of-the-art methods on two UAV-based RGB-T tiny pedestrian detection benchmarks while achieving real-time inference on the edge platform.

title: Self-prediction residuals improve single-pass detection of wrong-object boxes in grounded vision-language models
abstract: Grounded vision-language models write boxes as text, and the mean probability of their coordinate tokens says little about whether a box is right. We study a single-pass signal for boxes on another object, which matter when only the object counts. A linear map, fitted per model to its own answers without labels, reads a box from the hidden state before writing. Its disagreement with the written box, the self-prediction residual, flags boxes on another object although the read-out is far less accurate; the residual's weight was fixed with labels on two models. On a replication list of 1,200 RefCOCOg test items, the residual, averaged over six models, raises the detection of these errors for each of fifteen single-pass scores, by 0.026 to 0.049 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) on a label-free probe and probes trained on 2,000 labelled items. Over all errors, adding it to the label-free probe moves AUROC, averaged over the models, by less than 0.02 (95% interval). With a fifth of answers reviewed, the share of all errors caught moves from 0.518 to 0.524, that of boxes on another object from 0.505 to 0.607 (post hoc): the residual changes which errors are found, not how many, and in cost-weighted recall it breaks even when such a box costs about 0.86 times another error, and its gain is positive in point estimate at equal costs. These gains come from RefCOCOg lists of MS-COCO images.

title: Twisted Block Particle Filters: A Local Particle-System Change of Measure for High-Dimensional State-Space Models
abstract: Block particle filters mitigate weight degeneracy in high-dimensional state-space models, but their normalizer estimates can remain highly variable. We introduce a twisted block particle filter (TBPF) that incorporates predictive guidance through an exact change of measure at blockwise resampling. The method guide-tilts one uniformly selected offspring per block, leaves the state-transition kernel unchanged, and computes the resampling correction using finite empirical guide averages. title: Seeing 3D Occupancy Through Scene-Adaptive Projection
abstract: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction infers voxel-wise geometry and semantics from multi-view images, where 2D-to-3D view transformation is a crucial step. Many existing methods adopt a backward-projection paradigm, projecting uniformly distributed 3D reference points onto image planes to aggregate multi-view features. However, their scene-agnostic sampling patterns overlook the non-uniform distribution of scene geometry, allocating many references to empty space and reducing sampling efficiency under a fixed sampling budget. To address this challenge, we propose SAP, a scene-adaptive projection framework that leverages depth-based geometric priors to guide view transformation. Specifically, we back-project metric depth maps predicted by a frozen depth model into 3D space to obtain geometric priors. To leverage these priors, we design a Scene-Adaptive Projection Encoder comprising two complementary components. First, Prior-Guided Reference Generation constructs a hybrid reference set for feature sampling, allocating references within prior-supported height regions and retaining full-range sampling where valid support is unavailable. Furthermore, to account for potential spatial misalignment caused by depth estimation errors, Radial-Structured Feature Aggregation explores multiple candidate locations through learned radial offsets to aggregate potentially displaced feature evidence. Extensive experiments on Occ3D demonstrate that SAP achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently improves results across diverse occupancy frameworks.

title: Relative periodic orbits of a free spinning loop
abstract: A closed elastic string with no external forces can hold any shape while its material moves steadily along the curve (a steady axial motion), because its tension and the force needed to turn the material around a bend are both proportional to the curvature. I compute the periodic motions that grow from the simplest of these motions, the spinning ring, by Newton's method on a chain of masses. They include rotating waves that turn at twice the rotation rate of the material, standing "flappers" with two to five lobes, and period-doubled and period-tripled orbits. The chain only approximates the string. The orbits and their strong instabilities change little with more masses and are properties of the continuous string. Most weak instabilities change with the number of masses and are artifacts of approximating the string by a finite chain. The saddle flapper of a loop stretched 30% beyond its natural length is neutrally stable at small heights and unstable at large ones. Near a stretch of 1/12 the saddle flapper resonates with the breathing of the ring. Below that stretch the flapper slows as it grows and above it the flapper speeds up, and near the resonance two families of saddle flappers overlap. An unstable saddle flapper trades energy back and forth with an in-plane oval, and at large amplitude the energy spreads to the shortest waves of the chain. For Keller's linear string, whose tension is proportional to the stretched length, every motion is periodic, and every knot carries an exactly periodic flapper. For a Hookean string the curvature of a knot couples a ripple to stretching waves that travel at a different speed, and in the simulations a ripple on a sliding knot does not return to its starting shape. Whether a Hookean knot carries any periodic flapper is open.

title: EA-Bench: Measuring information and action efficiency under imperfect instructions
abstract: Personal agents help users complete everyday work across digital applications. Many standard benchmarks assume that users provide sufficient information to solve a task. However, agents often encounter incomplete, distracting, or inconsistent information in practice. To systematically study agent inefficiency under such imperfect information, we introduce Efficient Action (EA)-Bench, which evaluates both tool calls and user interactions in work-related tasks. To our knowledge, it is the first benchmark to jointly evaluate tool-call efficiency and user-interaction efficiency under controlled missing, redundant, and conflicting information. We construct 63 base-task instances adapted from existing work-related benchmarks. To guide perturbation design and quantify task requirements, we represent workflows as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and examine node-level dependencies to identify where information can be withheld, contradicted, or supplemented with distractors. We use a two-stage validation process combining AI-assisted checks with expert screening to select 232 conditions from 792 initial candidates. We organize these tasks into Easy and Hard tracks by task complexity. Experiments show that imperfect information can reduce accuracy and increase tool-use and user-interaction costs. More concerning, several models obtain apparently correct outcomes by guessing user-specific values without confirmation, revealing potential execution unreliability in current models under imperfect user information.
